frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Brembo investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B and aftermarket offerings, and identify what evidence would support that investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources; financial and contractual detail may not be available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Need to discover Brembo’s current reach to individual buyers and any existing consumer products.
Evidence must address demand, willingness to pay, competitive landscape, and feasibility of a new consumer proposition.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., high‑performance motorcycle brakes sold directly to enthusiasts).
2) Expand into a new consumer segment without differentiation (e.g., sell existing aftermarket parts through new retail channels).
3) No expansion – maintain current B2B and aftermarket focus.
4) License Brembo’s technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than selling under its own brand.
5) Partner with established consumer brands to co‑brand premium brake kits for specific enthusiast segments.

T1.claim: Enthusiast motorcyclists will purchase premium Brembo brakes directly because they value performance and brand heritage, and are willing to pay a premium for proven motorsport technology.
T1.who_benefits: Brembo benefits by capturing higher-margin sales of premium brake kits to individual enthusiasts.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Motorcyclists seek performance upgrades that demonstrate their passion and affiliation with professional racing; they trust Brembo's motorsport pedigree and are willing to pay more for a product that signals expertise.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Brembo sells directly to enthusiasts at premium prices, retaining the full retail margin rather than selling through intermediaries.
assumptions: Motorcyclists have sufficient disposable income to afford premium brake upgrades.
Brand awareness of Brembo's motorsport history is strong among enthusiasts.
Direct-to-consumer sales channels are feasible and cost-effective for Brembo.
predictions: If offered a premium Brembo brake kit priced at €750, at least 10% of surveyed enthusiasts will express intent to purchase.
Sales of the premium kit will generate higher per-unit revenue than aftermarket replacement parts.
T1.first_claim: Enthusiast motorcyclists will purchase premium Brembo brakes directly because they value performance and brand heritage, and are willing to pay a premium for proven motorsport technology.

T2.claim: Consumers will purchase Brembo brakes for urban and everyday use because they seek reliable, high‑performance braking solutions that enhance safety and convenience, and are willing to pay a premium for a brand associated with quality and innovation.
T2.who_benefits: Brembo benefits by expanding its consumer base into urban and everyday segments, capturing higher‑margin sales of lifestyle‑branded kits and potentially licensing its technology to third‑party consumer brands.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers prioritize safety and performance in daily driving and urban mobility; they trust Brembo's reputation for engineering excellence and are willing to pay more for a product that signals modern, tech‑savvy lifestyle.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Brembo sells premium lifestyle kits directly or through licensed partners at higher prices, retaining margin and building brand equity beyond its core automotive B2B business.
assumptions: Urban and everyday drivers have sufficient disposable income to afford premium brake upgrades.
Brand awareness of Brembo's technological leadership is growing among non‑motorcycle enthusiasts.
Lifestyle branding effectively communicates performance and heritage to non‑technical consumers.
predictions: If offered a lifestyle‑branded Brembo brake kit priced at €300 for urban use, at least 15% of surveyed urban drivers will express intent to purchase.
Sales of the lifestyle kit will generate higher per‑unit revenue than standard aftermarket parts.
T2.first_claim: Consumers will purchase Brembo brakes for urban and everyday use because they seek reliable, high‑performance braking solutions that enhance safety and convenience, and are willing to pay a premium for a brand associated with quality and innovation.

X1.name: Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Enthusiast vs Lifestyle Kits
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a premium enthusiast brake kit priced at €750; Group B sees a lifestyle-branded brake kit priced at €300. Both groups are asked about purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and willingness to pay (open‑ended).
X1.sample: 200 participants: 100 motorcycle enthusiasts (recruited via biker forums) and 100 urban drivers (recruited via general consumer panels).
X1.measure: Average purchase intent score for each group and the difference between the two groups.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will show higher average purchase intent and willingness to pay than Group B.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will show higher average purchase intent and willingness to pay than Group A.

X1.decision_rule: If Group A’s average purchase intent is at least 10 percentage points higher than Group B’s, T1 is supported. If Group B’s average purchase intent is at least 10 percentage points higher than Group A’s, T2 is supported. If the difference is less than 10 points, both theories remain uncertain.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns warehouse packing efficiency and does not address consumer demand, willingness to pay, or enthusiast purchasing behavior. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting enthusiast motorcyclists, but first validate demand and willingness to pay through a low‑cost willingness‑to‑pay survey before committing to full product development or marketing. The survey will test whether enthusiasts are willing to pay €750 for a premium heritage‑branded brake kit, which would support T1, or whether a lower‑priced lifestyle kit would be
final.target_customer: Enthusiast motorcyclists who value performance and motorsport heritage and are willing to pay a premium for proven racing‑derived products.
final.value_proposition: A premium, heritage‑branded brake kit that combines Brembo’s motorsport pedigree with advanced adjustability and adjustability, sold directly to enthusiasts at a price point that reflects premium positioning.
final.next_action: Run the proposed willingness‑to‑pay survey (200 participants, €15,000, 10 weeks) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a €750 enthusiast kit versus a €300 lifestyle kit.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer demand and willingness to pay for premium enthusiast kits. The survey will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the survey shows that at least 10% of enthusiasts express intent to purchase the €750 kit and willingness to pay that price, T1 would be supported and the recommendation would shift to full product development for enthusiasts.

If the survey shows that the €300 lifestyle kit generates higher intent and willingness to pay among enthusiasts, T2 would be supported and the recommendation would shift to a broader urban/everyday consumer proposition.

arguments.claim: Enthusiast motorcyclists will purchase premium Brembo brakes directly because they value performance and brand heritage, and are willing to pay a premium for proven motorsport technology.
arguments.who_benefits: Brembo benefits by capturing higher-margin sales of premium brake kits to individual enthusiasts.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Motorcyclists seek performance upgrades that demonstrate their passion and affiliation with professional racing; they trust Brembo's motorsport pedigree and are willing to pay more for a product that signals expertise.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Brembo sells directly to enthusiasts at premium prices, retaining the full retail margin rather than selling through intermediaries.
assumptions: Motorcyclists have sufficient disposable income to afford premium brake upgrades.
Brand awareness of Brembo's motorsport history is strong among enthusiasts.
Direct-to-consumer sales channels are feasible and cost-effective for Brembo.
predictions: If offered a premium Brembo brake kit priced at €750, at least 10% of surveyed enthusiasts will express intent to purchase.
Sales of the premium kit will generate higher per-unit revenue than aftermarket replacement parts.

arguments.claim: Consumers will purchase Brembo brakes for urban and everyday use because they seek reliable, high‑performance braking solutions that enhance safety and convenience, and are willing to pay a premium for a brand associated with quality and innovation.

arguments.how_value_is_captured: Brembo sells premium lifestyle kits directly or through licensed partners at higher prices, retaining margin and building brand equity beyond its core automotive B2B business.
assumptions: Urban and everyday drivers have sufficient disposable income to afford premium brake upgrades.
Brand awareness of Brembo's technological leadership is growing among non‑motorcycle enthusiasts.
Lifestyle branding effectively communicates performance and heritage to non‑technical consumers.
predictions: If offered a lifestyle‑branded Brembo brake kit priced at €300 for urban use, at least 15% of surveyed urban drivers will express intent to purchase.
Sales of the lifestyle kit will generate higher per‑unit revenue than standard aftermarket parts.

arguments.name: Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Enthusiast vs Lifestyle Kits
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a premium enthusiast brake kit priced at €750; Group B sees a lifestyle-branded brake kit priced at €300. Both groups are asked about purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and willingness to pay (open‑ended).
arguments.sample: 200 participants: 100 motorcycle enthusiasts (recruited via biker forums) and 100 urban drivers (recruited via general consumer panels).
arguments.measure: Average purchase intent score for each group and the difference between the two groups.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will show higher average purchase intent and willingness to pay than Group B.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will show higher average purchase intent and willingness to pay than Group A.

arguments.decision_rule: If Group A’s average purchase intent is at least 10 percentage points higher than Group B’s, T1 is supported. If Group B’s average purchase intent is at least 10 percentage points higher than Group A’s, T2 is supported. If the difference is less than 10 points, both theories remain uncertain.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Rieter Holding AG investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current industrial spinning machines, components, and after-sales services.
constraints: Limited to public sources; internal financial and contractual detail may not be available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Need to discover Rieter’s current reach to individual buyers and identify a specific consumer use case with measurable demand.
Evidence must demonstrate that a consumer proposition would generate value for Rieter, not just for end‑users.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home textile spinning, hobbyist yarn production) with a new product or service.
2) Expand Rieter’s existing B2B offerings into adjacent industrial segments (e.g., specialty fibers, sustainable spinning) without creating a consumer proposition.
3) Maintain the current business model with no expansion (status quo).
4) License Rieter technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than selling under Rieter’s own brand.
5) Partner with existing consumer brands to co‑develop a consumer‑focused spinning solution.

T1.claim: Hobbyists and small-scale creators will adopt Rieter’s entry-level spinning machines because they seek affordable automation and speed to increase productivity and enable creative experimentation.
T1.who_benefits: Hobbyists, hand spinners, and small-space creators who want to produce yarn for personal projects or small-batch sales.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: These users currently face high entry barriers (cost, complexity) and limited options for automated spinning. A low‑cost, easy‑to‑use machine would reduce the perceived barrier and increase willingness to purchase.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Rieter would capture value by selling a differentiated consumer product at a modest margin, leveraging its existing technology and service relationships with spinning mills.
assumptions: Hobbyists and small creators represent a significant, growing market segment.
They are willing to invest in equipment that reduces time and effort.
Rieter can design a simple, affordable machine without compromising quality.
predictions: If offered, hobbyists will purchase the machine at a price point below CHF 5,000.
Sales will be concentrated in regions with strong craft and DIY cultures (e.g., North America, Western Europe).
Customer satisfaction will be high, leading to repeat purchases and referrals.

T2.why_behaviour_changes: These users currently rely on manual or small‑scale equipment that limits output and consistency. A machine that offers incremental scalability and compatibility with existing spinning mills would reduce the perceived risk of over‑investing
T2.how_value_is_captured: Rieter would capture value by selling a modular system that can be expanded with additional modules, earning recurring revenue from upgrades and service contracts.
assumptions: Hobbyists and small producers have a demonstrated willingness to invest in equipment that supports growth.
They value interoperability with existing spinning mill infrastructure.
The market for small‑batch yarn production is growing due to craft trends and online distribution.
predictions: If offered, enthusiasts will purchase the base machine and later purchase expansion modules within 12 months.
Purchase decisions will be influenced by the ability to scale production without replacing the entire system.
Customer retention will be high due to the modularity that allows future upgrades.

X1.name: Hobbyist vs Enthusiast Purchase Intent Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated product offering and purchase intent questions.
X1.sample: 500 participants: 250 self‑identified hobbyists (craft, DIY, home spinning) and 250 self‑identified spinning enthusiasts (small‑batch yarn producers, fiber artists, professional spinners). Recruited via hobbyist forums, craft communities, and spinning enthusiast groups.
X1.measure: Purchase intent: "Would you buy this machine at the offered price?" (binary: Yes/No). Secondary: willingness to pay (open amount).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Hobbyists will show purchase intent at a price point below CHF 5,000, while enthusiasts will show lower intent or price sensitivity.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Enthusiasts will show purchase intent at a price point above CHF 5,000 and will indicate willingness to scale with expansion modules, while hobbyists will show lower intent or price sensitivity.

X1.decision_rule: If hobbyists show purchase intent at <30% and enthusiasts show intent at ≥30%, proceed with hobbyist‑focused consumer proposition. If both groups show intent at ≥30%, consider a dual‑segment approach. If neither group shows intent at ≥30%,

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer and packing errors, which does not address consumer demand, pricing, or purchase intent for Rieter's entry-level spinning machines. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Conduct the proposed hobbyist vs enthusiast purchase intent test to gather real demand data before committing resources. If the test confirms purchase intent above 30% for hobbyists at a price point below CHF 5,000, proceed with a hobbyist-focused consumer proposition; otherwise, maintain the current B2B model.
final.target_customer: Hobbyists and small-scale creators who need affordable automation and speed for personal projects or small-batch sales.
final.value_proposition: A low-cost, entry-level spinning machine that reduces time and effort for hobbyists, enabling creative experimentation and modest production.
final.next_action: Run the hobbyist vs enthusiast purchase intent test (10 weeks, €15,000 budget). If the test shows ≥30% intent for hobbyists at the offered price, proceed to develop the consumer proposition; otherwise, keep the current B2B model.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 are uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer demand and pricing. The test will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows <30% intent for hobbyists at the offered price, the favoured theory would shift to T2 and the recommendation would be to pursue a dual-segment approach or license the technology to third-party brands.

If new data shows a large, willing hobbyist market with purchase intent above 30% at a price point below CHF 5,000, T1 would become likely and the recommendation would shift to developing the consumer proposition.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Rieter Holding AG investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current industrial spinning machines, components, and after-sales services.
constraints: Limited to public sources; internal financial and contractual detail may not be available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Need to discover Rieter’s current reach to individual buyers and identify a specific consumer use case with measurable demand.
Evidence must demonstrate that a consumer proposition would generate value for Rieter, not just for end‑users.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home textile spinning, hobbyist yarn production) with a new product or service.
2) Expand Rieter’s existing B2B offerings into adjacent industrial segments (e.g., specialty fibers, sustainable spinning) without creating a consumer proposition.
3) Maintain the current business model with no expansion (status quo).
4) License Rieter technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than selling under Rieter’s own brand.
5) Partner with existing consumer brands to co‑develop a consumer‑focused spinning solution.

T1.claim: Hobbyists and small-scale creators will adopt Rieter’s entry-level spinning machines because they seek affordable automation and speed to increase productivity and enable creative experimentation.
T1.who_benefits: Hobbyists, hand spinners, and small-space creators who want to produce yarn for personal projects or small-batch sales.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: These users currently face high entry barriers (cost, learning curve) for traditional spinning. A low‑cost automated system reduces time and effort, making spinning accessible and rewarding.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Rieter captures value by selling machines under its own brand, charging a premium for integrated automation, and potentially offering consumables (fibers, accessories) and service contracts.
assumptions: Hobbyists and small creators have sufficient disposable income to purchase a machine.
They value speed and ease of use over maximum yield.
They are willing to pay a premium for a brand that simplifies the process.
predictions: A survey of hobbyists will show >30% would purchase a Rieter Artisan line within 12 months.
Sales of the Artisan line will be positively correlated with craft yarn market growth (e.g., CYC survey data).
Customer satisfaction scores will be high, indicating the machine meets their productivity needs.
T1.first_claim: Hobbyists and small-scale creators will adopt Rieter’s entry-level spinning machines because they seek affordable automation and speed to increase productivity and enable creative experimentation.

T2.claim: Spinning mill owners will adopt Rieter’s entry-level machines because they seek to reduce labor costs and increase production efficiency, leveraging Rieter’s automation to lower per‑unit costs.
T2.who_benefits: Spinning mills that produce staple fibers for textile manufacturers, seeking to lower operational expenses and increase throughput.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Mills currently face rising labor costs and competition from low‑cost producers. An automated spinning line reduces the need for skilled labor, allowing them to produce more yarn per shift and lower unit costs.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Rieter captures value by selling machines under its own brand, charging a premium for integrated automation, and potentially offering consumables (fibers, accessories) and service contracts that lower total cost of ownership.
assumptions: Mills have sufficient capital to invest in new equipment.
They prioritize cost reduction over other factors (e.g., yarn quality, brand association).
They trust Rieter’s technology to deliver measurable productivity gains.
predictions: A survey of spinning mill owners will show >25% would purchase the Artisan line within 12 months if price is competitive.
Sales of the Artisan line will be inversely correlated with labor costs in the region.
Mills will report higher throughput and lower per‑unit costs after installing the line.

X1.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with simulated purchase scenario.
X1.sample: 500 respondents: 250 hobbyists (crafters, spinners) and 250 spinning mill owners (mill managers, procurement officers).
X1.measure: Proportion of respondents who would purchase the Rieter Artisan line within 12 months at a specified price point.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Hobbyists' purchase intent ≥ 30% (threshold).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Mill owners' purchase intent ≥ 25% (threshold).

X1.decision_rule: If hobbyists' purchase intent ≥ 30% and mill owners' purchase intent ≥ 25%, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting hobbyists. If either group falls below 25%, abandon the consumer proposition.

final.recommendation: Proceed with a limited pilot of the Rieter Artisan line targeting hobbyists and small-scale creators, using the proposed choice-based conjoint survey to validate purchase intent. If the survey meets the 30% threshold for hobbyists, develop a differentiated consumer proposition; otherwise, maintain the current B2B focus.
final.target_customer: Hobbyists, hand spinners, and small-space creators who produce yarn for personal projects or small-batch sales.
final.value_proposition: A low‑cost automated spinning machine that reduces time and effort, enabling creative experimentation and affordable entry into yarn production.
final.next_action: Run the proposed 10‑week, €18,000 choice‑based conjoint survey with 500 respondents (250 hobbyists, 250 spinning mill owners). Calculate purchase intent for the Artisan line at a specified price point and compare against the 30% threshold.
final.uncertainty: The actual purchase intent of hobbyists and the market size for the Artisan line are unknown. The survey results will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the survey shows hobbyist purchase intent below 30%, the consumer proposition would be abandoned in favor of expanding B2B offerings.
If a separate test shows mill owners purchase intent above 25%, T2 would become more likely and the strategy would shift to target them.

X1.name: DIY Sealant Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants view a product description of a Sika DIY sealant (easy-apply, professional-grade) and are asked: "How likely are you to purchase this product?" (1‑10 scale). They also indicate willingness to pay (WTP) on a 7‑point scale (e.g., €15‑20).
X1.sample: 300 DIY consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and self‑reported DIY experience.
X1.measure: Average purchase likelihood score and average WTP for the easy‑apply version versus a control version described as a standard contractor‑grade sealant.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Average purchase likelihood for easy‑apply version will be at least 20% higher than for control version, and WTP will be at least 10% higher.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Average purchase likelihood for easy‑apply version will be at least 20% higher than for control version, and WTP will be at least 15% higher.

X1.decision_rule: If the easy‑apply version’s average likelihood exceeds the control version’s by ≥ 20 points AND the WTP premium is ≥ 10% (or ≥ 15% for T2), then the theory is supported. Otherwise, the theory is rejected.

final.recommendation: Run the proposed DIY Sealant Messaging Test (X1) to empirically compare consumer willingness to pay and purchase intent for a product marketed as "Easy-Apply Sealant for Home Repairs" versus a standard contractor-grade sealant. The test will determine whether the easy-apply positioning drives a meaningful premium and aligns with consumer behavior, which is essential before any investment.
final.target_customer: DIY consumers (homeowners or hobbyists) who need reliable performance without professional expertise and are willing to pay a small premium for convenience.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated DIY-focused product that is marketed as convenient, easy-to-use, and professional-grade, sold through existing retail channels, offering a modest premium over basic contractor-grade sealants.
final.next_action: Execute the 10‑week, €15,000 online survey test (X1) with 300 DIY consumers, measuring purchase likelihood and willingness to pay for the easy‑apply version versus a control version described as a standard contractor‑grade sealant.
final.uncertainty: Both theories remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer willingness to pay a premium for convenience or status. The test will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows the easy‑apply version’s average likelihood is at least 20 points higher than the control and the average WTP premium is at least 10% (or 15% for T2), the favoured theory would shift to support that mechanism.
If the test fails to show a meaningful premium or if the results contradict the theories, the recommendation would shift toward no expansion or a different approach.

arguments.name: DIY Sealant Messaging Test
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants view a product description of a Sika DIY sealant (easy-apply, professional-grade) and are asked: "How likely are you to purchase this product?" (1‑10 scale). They also indicate willingness to pay (WTP) on a 7‑point scale (e.g., €15‑20).
arguments.sample: 300 DIY consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and self‑reported DIY experience.
arguments.measure: Average purchase likelihood score and average WTP for the easy‑apply version versus a control version described as a standard contractor‑grade sealant.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Average purchase likelihood for easy‑apply version will be at least 20% higher than for control version, and WTP will be at least 10% higher.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Average purchase likelihood for easy‑apply version will be at least 20% higher than for control version, and WTP will be at least 15% higher.

arguments.decision_rule: If the easy‑apply version’s average likelihood exceeds the control version’s by ≥ 20 points AND the WTP premium is ≥ 10% (or ≥ 15% for T2), then the theory is supported. Otherwise, the theory is rejected.

position.recommendation: Run the proposed Consumer Choice Test (X1) to empirically compare purchase intent and willingness to pay for a premium branded sealant versus a convenience kit. The test will decide whether to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting premium-performance DIY users or pursue a bundled convenience kit approach. The test budget of €15,000 and 12‑week timeline are within the analyst’s constraints.

frame.objective: Determine whether Sika AG should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B construction chemicals, sealants, and adhesives, and identify what evidence would justify that investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources; internal company data may not be available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Need to discover Sika’s current reach to individual buyers and any existing consumer products.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, and a viable route to consumers for a new proposition.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., DIY waterproofing, home flooring adhesive) with a new brand and distribution channel.
2) Expand existing B2B offerings into new consumer segments via existing distribution (e.g., contractor‑to‑consumer sales) without creating a separate consumer brand.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current B2B construction chemicals, sealants, and adhesives.
4) License Sika’s technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than selling under Sika’s own consumer brand.
5) Partner with retailers to co‑brand Sika products for consumer use, leveraging existing retail relationships.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt Sika’s DIY sealants if they perceive them as easy‑to‑use, professional‑grade, and offering clear performance benefits (e.g., waterproofing, durability) that are demonstrably better than generic alternatives.
T1.who_benefits: DIY homeowners seeking reliable, high‑performance solutions for home improvement projects.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If consumers trust Sika’s brand reputation for professional quality and see clear performance advantages, they will choose Sika over generic or lower‑cost alternatives, even if the price is higher.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Sika can charge premium prices for branded DIY sealants, sell through existing retail channels (e.g., hardware stores, online), and leverage its existing distribution network to reach consumers directly.
assumptions: Consumers research product performance before purchase.
Brand trust and perceived professional quality are key purchase drivers for DIY sealants.
Sika can communicate clear performance benefits effectively to consumers.
predictions: In a test offering a Sika’ branded DIY sealant at a price 20% above generic alternatives, purchase intent among DIY shoppers will be at least 15% higher than for a generic product.
Surveyed consumers will rank Sika’s sealant higher on a 7‑point performance scale compared to a generic competitor.

T2.who_benefits: DIY homeowners who value speed and simplicity in project completion.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: If consumers perceive Sika as a one‑stop shop that simplifies the buying process and reduces decision‑making time, they will choose Sika even if the price is comparable to generic alternatives.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Sika can charge a premium for a bundled DIY kit, sell through existing retail channels (e.g., hardware stores, online), and leverage its distribution network to offer a convenient purchase experience.
assumptions: Consumers prioritize time‑saving and convenience over price for small‑scale projects.
Sika can package multiple sealants into a single kit without compromising performance.
Retail partners will stock a bundled kit rather than separate products.
predictions: In a test offering a Sika’branded DIY kit (e.g., sealant, adhesive, primer) at a price comparable to generic alternatives, purchase intent among DIY shoppers will be at least 10% higher than for a generic kit.
Surveyed consumers will rank Sika’s kit higher on a 7‑point convenience scale compared to a generic competitor.

Participants view two Sika DIY sealant options: (1) Premium branded sealant (e.g., Sikaflex) priced 20% above a generic alternative, marketed as professional‑grade, easy‑to‑use, and offering clear performance benefits; (2) Convenience kit (sealant + primer + adhesive) priced at a comparable price to generic alternatives, marketed as a single‑source solution that saves time and effort. X1.sample: 300 DIY homeowners recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and DIY experience. Randomly assigned to view either the premium sealant or the convenience kit.
X1.measure: Purchase intent measured on a 7‑point scale (1‑Very unlikely to 7‑Very likely). Secondary measure: willingness to pay a premium (20% above generic) for the premium sealant.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Participants viewing the premium sealant will show purchase intent at least 15% higher than those viewing the convenience kit, and willingness to pay a premium will be at least 10% higher.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Participants viewing the convenience kit will show purchase intent at least 15% higher than those viewing the premium sealant, and no significant difference in willingness to pay a premium.

final.target_customer: DIY homeowners seeking reliable, high‑performance sealants for home improvement projects.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated consumer brand offering Sika’s professional‑grade sealants with clear performance benefits, sold through existing retail channels at a premium price.
final.next_action: Execute the Consumer Choice Test (X1) with 300 DIY homeowners, measuring purchase intent and willingness to pay for the premium sealant versus a convenience kit.
final.uncertainty: Both theories remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer willingness to pay a premium for Sika or for convenience. The test will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows the convenience kit group’s purchase intent is at least 15 percentage points higher than the premium sealant group, we would recommend pursuing a bundled convenience kit approach rather than a premium brand.

If the premium sealant group’s purchase intent is at least 15 percentage points higher and willingness to pay a premium is demonstrated, we would proceed with the differentiated consumer proposition targeting premium‑performance DIY users.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify TOMRA Systems ASA investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B offerings (reverse vending machines for deposit return systems and sensor-based sorting machines for waste, metal recycling, mining, and food processing).

alternatives: 1) Develop a consumer‑facing reverse vending machine for individual household use (e.g., home recycling of plastic bottles).

3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on existing B2B customers (retailers, deposit system operators, recyclers, mining, food processors).
4) Target a new consumer segment such as schools, offices, or apartment buildings with a shared recycling system using TOMRA sensors.

position.recommendation: Run the proposed Home Reverse Vending vs Subscription Sorting Test (X1) to empirically compare consumer adoption of a home reverse vending machine versus a subscription sorting service. frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify TOMRA Systems ASA investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B offerings (reverse vending machines for deposit return systems and sensor-based sorting machines for waste, metal recycling, mining, and food processing).
constraints: Limited to public sources; financial and contractual detail may not be available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Need to verify current reach to individual buyers and identify specific consumer use cases.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or a clear value capture mechanism for the manufacturer.
alternatives: 1) Develop a consumer‑facing reverse vending machine for individual household use (e.g., home recycling of plastic bottles).
2) Create a subscription‑based recycling service for consumers that uses TOMRA sensors to sort waste at home.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on existing B2B customers (retailers, deposit system operators, recyclers, mining, food processors).
4) Target a new consumer segment such as schools, offices, or apartment buildings with a shared recycling system using TOMRA sensors.
5) Introduce a consumer product that leverages TOMRA’s sensor technology for smart sorting of mixed waste (e.g., a consumer compactor that identifies recyclable materials).

T1.how_value_is_captured: TOMRA captures value by selling the machine to consumers and earning service fees from retailers or deposit system operators who use the machine.
assumptions: Consumers trust that the refund will be paid.
The price of the machine is affordable for the target demographic.
There is sufficient awareness of the product among potential buyers.
predictions: If offered a home reverse vending machine, a significant portion of households with plastic bottle consumption will register and use the machine regularly.
Surveyed consumers will indicate higher recycling rates compared to baseline data.

arguments.name: Digital Refund vs Eco-Friendly Consumer Pilot
arguments.method: Run two parallel pilot programs in two distinct consumer segments: (1) a convenience-focused group (e.g., apartment building residents) offered a digital refund app with deposit return; (2) an eco-focused group offered a sensor-sorted mixed-waste collection service. Both pilots operate for 12 weeks, with weekly usage data collected.
arguments.sample: 100 households in each segment (200 total) recruited via local community boards and online panels. Each household receives a unique code to access the respective pilot service.
arguments.measure: Number of refund transactions initiated via the digital app per household per week; and number of sensor-sorted waste collections per household per week.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Digital refund adoption rate will be at least 15% of households per week (i.e., at least 15 households initiating a refund transaction).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Eco-friendly adoption rate will be at least 10% of households per week (i.e., at least 10 households initiating a sensor-sorted collection).

arguments.decision_rule: If digital refund adoption rate ≥ 15% AND eco-friendly adoption rate ≤ 10%, then T1 is supported. If eco-friendly adoption rate ≥ 15% AND digital refund adoption rate ≤ 10%, then T2 is supported. If both rates meet their respective thresholds, both theories are supported. If neither meets its threshold, both theories are rejected.

They are asked about willingness to pay a 20% premium over a generic competitor and their likelihood to purchase. The test also measures perceived importance of each benefit.
X1.sample: 400 German adults who own or regularly drive a vehicle (recruited via panel). Stratified by age and vehicle type to reflect Eberspächer’s target segments.
X1.measure: 1) Average willingness to pay premium (euros) for the premium‑messaging version vs generic version. 2) Purchase intent (percentage saying “Very likely to buy”) for each messaging version. 3) Importance ranking of performance/safety vs convenience.

prediction_by_theory.T2: Convenience messaging will generate at least 10% higher willingness to pay and purchase intent than generic messaging, and importance ranking of convenience will be higher.

result.title: Simulated parking-heater installation offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited camper-van and motorhome owners interested in a diesel parking heater were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical heater, brand, heat output, total installed price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included fitting by a certified mobile technician at the owner's home on a booked date; the other required the owner to book the same fitting at a dealer workshop. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the mobile-fitting offer and 32 for the workshop offer. This tests whether installation friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at today's prices, that mobile fitting can be staffed or earns a margin, or that it would win buyers from cheaper self-fitted heaters. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

result.title: Simulated parking-heater installation offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited camper-van and motorhome owners interested in a diesel parking heater were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical heater, brand, heat output, total installed price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included fitting by a certified mobile technician at the owner's home on a booked date; the other required the owner to book the same fitting at a dealer workshop. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the mobile-fitting offer and 32 for the workshop offer. This tests whether installation friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at today's prices, that mobile fitting can be staffed or earns a margin, or that it would win buyers from cheaper self-fitted heaters. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

tool_result.title: Simulated parking-heater installation offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited camper-van and motorhome owners interested in a diesel parking heater were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical heater, brand, heat output, total installed price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included fitting by a certified mobile technician at the owner's home on a booked date; the other required the owner to book the same fitting at a dealer workshop. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the mobile-fitting offer and 32 for the workshop offer. This tests whether installation friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at today's prices, that mobile fitting can be staffed or earns a margin, or that it would win buyers from cheaper self-fitted heaters. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

position.recommendation: Run the proposed Premium vs. Compliance Messaging Choice Test (X1) to empirically compare willingness to pay for premium versus compliance-driven messaging among boat owners and EV owners. The test will determine which segment shows a meaningful premium premium and which segment shows minimal difference, helping to decide whether to pursue a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case.

frame.objective: Determine whether Eberspächer Gruppe GmbH & Co. KG should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B exhaust technology, vehicle heaters, and thermal management systems, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; internal financial and contractual detail may not be available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current reach to individual buyers is unknown; must be discovered.
Investment must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and ability to capture value.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product for a specific use case (e.g., electric vehicle (EV) thermal management, home charging heaters, or a new consumer brand).
2) Expand the existing B2B portfolio with new consumer‑facing features or services without creating a separate consumer brand (e.g., aftermarket EV heater kits, consumer‑friendly exhaust components).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current B2B markets and existing product lines.
4) Partner with or license technology to existing consumer brands rather than creating a new consumer proposition.
5) Target a different customer segment (e.g., individual consumers vs. fleet operators) with the same core product, possibly via a new distribution channel.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive it as a premium, convenient, and status-enhancing product, especially for niche markets like recreational boating or electric vehicle (EV) thermal management.
T1.who_benefits: Individual consumers seeking comfort, convenience, and status; Eberspächer benefits by capturing higher margins and brand differentiation.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If consumers view the product as a necessary luxury that improves comfort and experience, they are willing to pay more and purchase directly, bypassing traditional B2B dealers.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Eberspächer captures value through premium pricing, direct-to-consumer sales, and brand association that differentiates its products from generic competitors.
assumptions: Consumers in target niches are willing to pay a premium for comfort and status.
Marketing can effectively communicate the product's unique benefits to individual buyers.
Distribution channels (e.g., online, specialty retailers) can reach individual consumers at scale.
predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate willingness to pay at least 20% above standard B2B pricing for a differentiated consumer proposition.
Purchase intent will be higher among owners of recreational boats and EV owners compared to general vehicle owners.
Brand perception studies will show the proposition is associated with premium, reliable, and innovative features.
T1.first_claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive it as a premium, convenient, and status-enhancing product, especially for niche markets like recreational boating or electric vehicle (EV) thermal management.

T2.claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if regulatory or environmental pressures make a premium, efficient thermal management solution mandatory or financially advantageous, especially for electric vehicles (EVs).
T2.who_benefits: Individual EV owners and fleet operators who must meet emissions or efficiency standards; Eberspächer benefits by capturing demand for certified, high‑performance components.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Regulatory requirements or incentives (e.g., tax credits, emission credits) create a financial incentive to purchase advanced thermal management, making a premium product more attractive than generic alternatives.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Eberspächer captures value through premium pricing justified by certification, compliance benefits, and potential rebates or subsidies, positioning its products as a compliance‑ready solution.
assumptions: Regulatory bodies will enforce or incentivize advanced thermal management for EVs.
Consumers and fleet operators are aware of and prioritize compliance benefits.
Competitors will also offer certified solutions, maintaining price competition.
predictions: Surveyed EV owners will indicate willingness to pay at least 15% above standard B2B pricing for a certified, compliant thermal management kit.
Purchase intent will be higher in regions with stringent EV emission standards.
Brand perception studies will show the proposition is associated with compliance, reliability, and environmental responsibility.

X1.measure: Willingness to pay premium over standard B2B price (20% for boat owners, 15% for EV owners). Also measure purchase intent (1‑0 scale) and maximum price paid.

final.recommendation: Run the proposed Premium vs. Compliance Messaging Choice Test (X1) to empirically compare willingness to pay for premium versus compliance-driven messaging among boat owners and EV owners. final.value_proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes premium comfort, status, and convenience for recreational boating and EV thermal management, sold directly to individual buyers at a premium price.
final.next_action: Execute the 8‑week, €12,000 choice test with 400 participants (200 boat owners, 200 EV owners) to measure premium willingness to pay and purchase intent differences.
final.uncertainty: Both theories remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence of consumer demand for premium pricing or regulatory pressure. The test will resolve this uncertainty.

result.title: Simulated parking-heater installation offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited camper-van and motorhome owners interested in a diesel parking heater were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical heater, brand, heat output, total installed price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included fitting by a certified mobile technician at the owner's home on a booked date; the other required the owner to book the same fitting at a dealer workshop. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the mobile-fitting offer and 72 for the workshop offer. This tests whether installation friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at today's prices, that mobile fitting can be staffed or earns a margin, or that it would win buyers from cheaper self-fitted heaters. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

result.title: Simulated parking-heater installation offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited camper-van and motorhome owners interested in a diesel parking heater were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical heater, brand, heat output, total installed price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included fitting by a certified mobile technician at the owner's home on a booked date; the other required the owner to book the same fitting at a dealer workshop. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the mobile-fitting offer and 72 for the workshop offer. This tests whether installation friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at today's prices, that mobile fitting can be staffed or earns a margin, or that it would win buyers from cheaper self-fitted heaters. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

tool_result.title: Simulated parking-heater installation offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited camper-van and motorhome owners interested in a diesel parking heater were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical heater, brand, heat output, total installed price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included fitting by a certified mobile technician at the owner's home on a booked date; the other required the owner to book the same fitting at a dealer workshop. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the mobile-fitting offer and 72 for the workshop offer. This tests whether installation friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at today's prices, that mobile fitting can be staffed or earns a margin, or that it would win buyers from cheaper self-fitted heaters. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
tool_result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Gühring KG investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current industrial metal machining tools, and identify what evidence would support that investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources; financial and contractual detail may not be available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Need to discover Gühring’s current reach to individual buyers and any existing consumer products.
Evidence must address demand, willingness to pay, competitive landscape, and feasibility of reaching consumers.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., DIY metalworking, hobbyists, small workshops) with a new product line or marketing approach.
2) Expand the existing B2B product portfolio into adjacent industrial segments (e.g., aerospace, medical) without creating a consumer proposition.
3) No expansion: maintain current product and market focus, not pursuing new consumer or consumer‑focused initiatives.
4) License Gühring’s technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than selling under Gühring brand.
5) Partner with established consumer brands to co‑develop and distribute consumer‑focused tools, leveraging existing consumer channels.

T1.claim: Hobbyists and small workshops will adopt Gühring’s precision tools if they are marketed as premium, high‑performance solutions for specific, well‑defined use cases (e.g., metal fabrication, CNC machining), because hobbyists value quality and reliability over cost.
T1.who_benefits: Hobbyists and small workshop owners who need reliable, accurate tools for specific tasks.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If Gühring positions its tools as essential for professional‑grade results, hobbyists will perceive them as a necessary investment rather than a discretionary purchase.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Gühring would sell under its own brand at premium prices, capturing margin through direct‑to‑consumer sales or through authorized distributors who can emphasize quality.
assumptions: Hobbyists have sufficient disposable income to afford premium tools for specific tasks.
They are willing to pay more for tools that deliver consistent precision.
Marketing can effectively communicate the tool’s performance benefits to this segment.
predictions: Surveyed hobbyists will indicate intent to purchase Gühring tools for specific use cases at a price 20‑30% above standard industrial tools.
Pilot sales of a limited consumer line will generate at least 10% of total Gühring revenue within 12 months.
Customer satisfaction scores for the consumer line will be comparable to or exceed those of established hobbyist brands.

result.title: Simulated printer-nozzle durability offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 32 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

tool_result.title: Simulated printer-nozzle durability offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 32 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Gühring KG investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current industrial metal machining tools, and identify what evidence would support that investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources; financial and contractual detail may not be available.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., DIY metalworking, hobbyists, small workshops) with a new product line or marketing approach.
2) Expand the existing B2B product portfolio into adjacent industrial segments (e.g., aerospace, medical) without creating a consumer proposition.
3) No expansion: maintain current product and market focus, not pursuing new consumer or consumer‑focused initiatives.
4) License Gühring’s technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than selling under Gühring brand.
5) Partner with established consumer brands to co‑develop and distribute consumer‑focused tools, leveraging existing consumer channels.

X1.name: Hobbyist Purchase Intent Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated product listing and purchase decision. Participants are recruited from hobbyist forums and social media to represent small workshops and DIY metalworkers. They are shown a Gühring precision metalworking tool (e.g., a drill bit) with a price 20% above a generic competitor. They also see the same tool offered via Gühring’s existing B2B online shop (PunchOut interface) at the same price. Participants indicate whether they would purchase the tool and, if so, which channel they would use. The test runs for 12 weeks, with 500 participants per arm (1,000 total).
X1.sample: 500 hobbyists (estimated from forum membership and social media reach). Recruitment cost €2,000.
X1.measure: Purchase intent rate (percentage of participants who select "Yes" to buy) for the premium-priced tool. Secondary measure: channel preference (channel selected for purchase).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Premium-priced tool purchase intent ≥ 15% and channel preference for premium price is "Direct B2B" (Gühring shop).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Premium-priced tool purchase intent ≥ 15% and channel preference for premium price is "Direct B2B" (Gühring shop).

X1.decision_rule: If purchase intent for the premium tool is ≥ 15% and channel preference for the premium price is "Direct B2B" (Gühring shop), then both theories are supported and the investment case is justified. If either condition fails, the test is inconclusive.

revisions.reason: Simulated result SYN-GUEHRING-UPDATE concerns a durability guarantee for a 3D-printer nozzle, not metalworking tools. It does not address Gühring’s precision metalworking tools or hobbyist purchase behavior for those tools. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

final.recommendation: Run the proposed Hobbyist Purchase Intent Test (12 weeks, €20,000) to measure purchase intent for a premium-priced Gühring tool offered via the existing B2B online shop. If the test meets the 15% purchase intent threshold and shows channel preference for the B2B shop, the evidence will support T1 and justify investment in a differentiated consumer proposition for hobbyists. Otherwise, the test will be inconclusive.
final.target_customer: Hobbyist and small workshop metalworkers who need reliable, high‑accuracy cutting tools for metal projects.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes Gühring’s precision, durability, and ease of purchase through the existing B2B online shop, leveraging the PunchOut interface to simplify procurement for hobbyists.
final.next_action: Execute the Hobbyist Purchase Intent Test as described, monitor results against the 15% purchase intent threshold and channel preference for the B2B shop.
final.uncertainty: The current evidence base does not directly show that hobbyists would purchase Gühring tools at a premium price or that they are aware of the brand. The test is needed to verify demand and willingness to pay.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent below 15% or channel preference for competitors, the investment case would be weakened and alternative strategies would be considered.
If additional independent data shows strong hobbyist demand for Gühring tools or a willingness to pay a premium, the case would strengthen.

arguments.name: Hobbyist Purchase Intent Test
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated product listing and purchase decision. Participants are recruited from hobbyist forums and social media to represent small workshops and DIY metalworkers. They are shown a Gühring precision metalworking tool (e.g., a drill bit) with a price 20% above a generic competitor. They also see the same tool offered via Gühring’s existing B2B online shop (PunchOut interface) at the same price. Participants indicate whether they would purchase the tool and, if so, which channel they would use. The test runs for 12 weeks, with 500 participants per arm (1,000 total).
arguments.sample: 500 hobbyists (estimated from forum membership and social media reach). Recruitment cost €2,000.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent rate (percentage of participants who select "Yes" to buy) for the premium-priced tool. Secondary measure: channel preference (channel selected for purchase).

arguments.decision_rule: If purchase intent for the premium tool is ≥ 15% and channel preference for the premium price is "Direct B2B" (Gühring shop), then both theories are supported and the investment case is justified. If either condition fails, the test is inconclusive.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

result.title: Simulated printer-nozzle durability offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 32 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

result.title: Simulated printer-nozzle durability offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 72 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

tool_result.title: Simulated printer-nozzle durability offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 72 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Gühring KG investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current industrial metal machining tools, and identify what evidence would support that investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources; financial and contractual detail may not be available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Need to discover Gühring’s current reach to individual buyers and any existing consumer products.
Evidence must address demand, willingness to pay, competitive landscape, and feasibility of reaching consumers.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., DIY metalworking, hobbyists, small workshops) with a new product line or marketing approach.
2) Expand the existing B2B product portfolio into adjacent industrial segments (e.g., aerospace, medical) without creating a consumer proposition.
3) No expansion: maintain current product and market focus, not pursuing new consumer or consumer‑focused initiatives.
4) License Gühring’s technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than selling under Gühring brand.
5) Partner with established consumer brands to co‑develop and distribute consumer‑focused tools under a joint brand.

T1.claim: Hobbyists and small workshops will adopt Gühring’s precision tools if they are marketed as affordable, entry‑level solutions for metalworking, because these users value reliability and performance for small‑batch projects.
T1.who_benefits: Individual hobbyists and small workshops (DIY metalworkers, model makers, hobby CNC users) benefit from a low‑cost, reliable tool that meets their precision needs.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: These users currently avoid professional‑grade tools due to cost and perceived complexity. A clear, low‑price entry point would signal accessibility and reduce the perceived barrier to entry.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Gühring would capture value by selling under its own brand at modest margins, leveraging its existing distribution channels (online shop, B2B partners) to reach this segment.
assumptions: Hobbyists and small workshops currently purchase tools from generic or low‑cost brands.
Price is a primary purchase driver for this segment.
Gühring’s precision reputation transfers to hobbyist use cases.
predictions: If Gühring launches a dedicated hobbyist line with clear pricing, pre‑orders or early adopters will exceed a defined threshold within 12 weeks.
Surveyed hobbyists will indicate willingness to pay a price point 20‑30% above entry‑level competitors but below professional‑grade tools.
T1.first_claim: Hobbyists and small workshops will adopt Gühring’s precision tools if they are marketed as affordable, entry‑level solutions for metalworking, because these users value reliability and performance for small‑batch projects.

T2.claim: Hobbyists and small workshops will adopt Gühring’s tools if they are marketed as part of a community or subscription service that provides ongoing support, updates, and a platform for sharing projects, because these users value social interaction and continuous learning.
T2.who_benefits: Individual hobbyists and small workshops benefit from a supportive ecosystem that reduces the perceived risk of buying professional‑grade tools and provides a community for sharing knowledge and projects.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Currently, hobbyists purchase tools as isolated items without ongoing support. A community‑driven model would signal a shift from isolated purchases to a membership‑based relationship, making the high‑cost entry more acceptable.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Gühring would capture value through subscription fees, premium tool kits, and data services, while leveraging its existing distribution channels to offer the community platform.
assumptions: Hobbyists seek social interaction and project sharing beyond tool ownership.
A community platform can be integrated with Gühring’s existing tools and distribution.
Subscription retention rates are sufficient to justify the cost of community management.
predictions: If Gühring launches a community‑based subscription service with a defined community platform and pricing, the number of active subscribers will exceed a defined threshold within 12 weeks.

Surveyed hobbyists will indicate willingness to pay a subscription fee that includes access to a community, updates, and technical support, even if the base tool price is above entry‑level competitors.

arguments.why_behaviour_changes: These users currently avoid professional‑grade tools due to cost and perceived complexity. A clear, low‑price entry point would signal accessibility and reduce the perceived barrier to entry.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Gühring would capture value by selling under its own brand at modest margins, leveraging its existing distribution channels (online shop, B2B partners) to reach this segment.

result.title: Simulated printer-nozzle durability offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 72 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

tool_result.title: Simulated printer-nozzle durability offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 72 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

frame.objective: Determine whether Krones AG should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B product lines, and identify evidence that would justify that investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources; financial and contractual detail may not be available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be discovered.
Any recommendation must consider Krones’ existing product portfolio, market demand, competitive landscape, and potential value capture mechanisms.
alternatives: 1) Develop a consumer-facing product or service for a specific use case (e.g., home brewing, small‑batch food production) that Krones currently does not offer.
2) Expand Krones’ existing B2B offerings into new segments or geographies without creating a distinct consumer proposition.
3) No expansion: maintain the current product and market focus, not pursuing new consumer or consumer‑focused initiatives.
4) Partner with or license Krones technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than building a direct consumer proposition.

T1.claim: Home brewers and small batch food producers will purchase Krones-branded equipment to achieve premium quality and scale, creating demand for a differentiated consumer proposition.
T1.who_benefits: Consumers seeking high-quality, consistent results; small-batch producers needing reliable, scalable technology.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing interest in craft beer and specialty food production drives demand for machines that ensure consistent quality and enable batch production without compromising taste.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Krones would sell equipment directly to consumers or through a subscription model, capturing margins on hardware and consumables (e.g., brewing capsules).
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for quality and reliability.
Small batch producers have sufficient capital to invest in Krones equipment.
Krones can design a consumer-friendly, user‑friendly product.
Distribution channels can reach individual consumers or small businesses.
predictions: A dedicated consumer channel would generate at least 5% of Krones’ total sales within five years.
Customer satisfaction scores for consumer‑facing machines would be above 85% in surveys.

T2.claim: Krones will develop a differentiated consumer proposition to capture the growing market of hobbyist home brewers and small-batch food producers by offering a subscription model that delivers consumables (e.g., brewing capsules) and service, leveraging its existing B2B technology.

T2.why_behaviour_changes: Hobbyists and small producers value consistent quality and time-saving; they are willing to pay for a subscription that delivers pre-measured ingredients and support.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Krones sells a subscription kit (capsules, cleaning kit, and optional service) directly to consumers, capturing recurring revenue and margin on consumables.
assumptions: Consumers will adopt a subscription model for home brewing supplies.
Krones can produce consumables at scale without major retooling.
Distribution can reach individual consumers online or via retail partners.
Subscription churn rate is acceptable (e.g., 5% per year).
predictions: Subscription revenue will contribute at least 10% of Krones’ total sales within three years.
Customer retention rate for the subscription service will be above 80% after 12 months.
