X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Dedicated Channel vs Subscription
X1.method: Online survey experiment with simulated purchase options
X1.sample: 500 participants: 250 hobbyist home brewers/small-batch producers (recruited via brewing forums and social media), 250 general consumers (recruited via consumer panels). Randomly assign each participant to one of two scenarios.
X1.measure: Purchase intent measured by willingness-to-pay (WTP) and likelihood to purchase Krones-branded equipment in the given scenario.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Participants in the dedicated consumer channel scenario will show higher WTP and purchase intent than those in the subscription scenario, because they view Krones as a premium brand offering reliable quality.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Participants in the subscription scenario will show higher WTP and purchase intent than those in the dedicated channel scenario, because convenience and recurring consumables appeal to hobbyists.

X1.decision_rule: Calculate the difference in WTP between the two scenarios. If the difference is at least 15% (e.g., subscription WTP exceeds dedicated channel WTP by €200), proceed to develop the subscription model; otherwise, develop a dedicated consumer offering.

revisions.reason: Simulated result SYN-KRONES-UPDATE concerns cleaning burden and does not address consumer demand for Krones-branded equipment, premium quality, or willingness to pay for a dedicated channel. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

Use the 15% difference threshold to decide whether to develop a subscription model (proceed if subscription exceeds dedicated channel by ≥15%) or a dedicated consumer proposition (proceed if dedicated channel exceeds subscription by ≥15%). Until the test, maintain the current B2B-
final.target_customer: Hobbyist home brewers and small-batch food producers who value premium quality, consistency, and convenience.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition that offers Krones-branded equipment and consumables, emphasizing reliability, ease of use, and a subscription model for recurring revenue.
final.next_action: Execute the Consumer Preference Test (X1) within the 12‑week timeline and €20,000 budget, measuring willingness-to-pay and purchase intent for the two scenarios.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain due to limited public evidence on consumer demand for Krones-branded equipment and subscription models. The test will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows subscription WTP exceeds dedicated channel WTP by ≥15%, proceed to develop a subscription model.
If the test shows dedicated channel WTP exceeds subscription WTP by ≥15%, proceed to develop a dedicated consumer proposition.
If neither threshold is met, abandon expansion and maintain the current B2B focus.

result.title: Simulated compact-brewing-system cleaning offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 32 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that such a system could be built at a price these buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Krones' industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

tool_result.title: Simulated compact-brewing-system cleaning offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 32 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that such a system could be built at a price these buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Krones' industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

X1.method: Online survey with simulated product offering. Participants are recruited from a panel of home brewers and small-batch producers. They are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Condition A receives a description of a compact, affordable filling and packaging system emphasizing scalability and cost-effectiveness (aligned with T1). Condition B receives the same description plus a separate description emphasizing unique design, premium branding, and status signaling (aligned with T2). Both conditions include a
X1.sample: 200 participants (100 per condition) who have purchased home brewing equipment in the past 2 years and have at least 500 followers on a social media platform (to verify reach). Recruitment via a panel that matches demographic and geographic criteria.
X1.measure: Primary outcome: binary purchase intent (yes/no) within 12 weeks. Secondary outcomes: willingness to pay (WTP) on a 7-point scale and perceived importance of scalability vs status (1‑5 scale).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Condition A will achieve a purchase intent rate of at least 15% and a significantly higher WTP for scalability than status.

result.title: Simulated compact-brewing-system cleaning offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 72 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that such a system could be built at a price these buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Krones' industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

result.title: Simulated compact-brewing-system cleaning offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 72 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that such a system could be built at a price these buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Krones' industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

tool_result.title: Simulated compact-brewing-system cleaning offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 72 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that such a system could be built at a price these buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Krones' industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
tool_result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Ease of Installation vs Safety Compliance
X1.method: Online survey with simulated product pages for a limited consumer line of LAPP cables marketed for home automation. Participants view one version emphasizing ease of installation and compatibility with smart home platforms (T1) and another emphasizing safety compliance and building code certification (T2). Both versions include the same product description, price (€20 per unit), and a brief safety/installation explanation. Participants indicate which version they would choose and
X1.sample: 500 German homeowners and DIY enthusiasts recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and home‑automation experience.
X1.measure: Percentage of participants choosing the ease‑of‑installation version versus the safety‑compliance version.

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 60% of participants will choose the ease‑of‑installation version, indicating demand for convenience over safety compliance.
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 60% of participants will choose the safety‑compliance version, indicating demand for code‑compliant cables.

X1.decision_rule: If the chosen version for T1 exceeds 60% of participants, proceed with developing a consumer proposition focused on ease of installation and compatibility. If the chosen version for T2 exceeds 60%, proceed with developing a consumer proposition focused on safety compliance and

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-LAPP-UPDATE concerns compatibility uncertainty for electric-car charging cables, not safety compliance or building code requirements. It does not address T1's claim about consumer demand for ease of installation and compatibility in home automation. Therefore the evidence is neutral for T1 and does not affect its status.

final.recommendation: Run the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to measure demand for ease-of-installation versus safety-compliance messaging. If ≥60% choose the ease-of-installation version, develop a consumer proposition emphasizing convenience and compatibility; otherwise, focus on safety compliance. The test cost is €15,000 and takes 12 weeks, fitting the analyst budget and timeframe.
final.target_customer: German homeowners and DIY enthusiasts who need reliable, compatible cables for home automation.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated consumer line of LAPP cables marketed as easy-to-install, compatible with popular smart home platforms, sold directly at a premium price of €20 per unit.
final.next_action: Execute the Consumer Preference Test (X1) within 12 weeks, using the €15,000 budget to recruit 500 participants, run simulated product pages, and collect choice data.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer demand for either proposition. The test will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows ≥60% choose the safety-compliance version, the recommendation would shift to developing a consumer line emphasizing code compliance and safety certification.
If the test shows <40% choose either version, the recommendation would be to abandon consumer expansion and remain focused on the industrial machinery market.

result.title: Simulated home-charging compatibility offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical products, charging power, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added a free check of the owner's car model and home wiring with a written assurance that the set would work with both; the other listed the same compatibility tables for the owner to check. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 32 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

frame.objective: Determine whether U.I. Lapp GmbH should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current industrial machinery market, based on evidence of market demand, competitive landscape, and feasibility within the analyst’s test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe.
constraints: Limited to public sources; internal financial and contractual detail may not be available.

Investment must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and ability to capture value.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific consumer use case (e.g., home automation, automotive DIY, or consumer electronics assembly).

4) License LAPP’s technology to consumer brands or create a white‑label consumer product line while retaining the core industrial business.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt LAPP’s consumer products if they perceive them as safe, reliable, and easy to install, because safety and ease of use are primary purchase drivers for electromobility accessories.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: Safety concerns (e.g., fire risk, electrical failure) and installation complexity deter consumers from purchasing generic accessories; a brand known for industrial reliability reduces perceived risk.
T1.how_value_is_captured: LAPP can charge premium prices for safety‑certified, easy‑to‑install products and sell directly through its online shop, capturing margin on each unit.
assumptions: Consumers research product safety ratings before purchase.
LAPP’s industrial reputation transfers to consumer perception of safety.
Installation ease is a significant barrier for non‑professional users.
predictions: In a test offering a safety‑certified, easy‑to‑install wallbox at a price 15% above generic competitors, purchase intent among drivers who cite safety as a top concern will be at least 20% higher than for a generic product.

result.title: Simulated home-charging compatibility offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical products, charging power, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added a free check of the owner's car model and home wiring with a written assurance that the set would work with both; the other listed the same compatibility tables for the owner to check. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 32 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

tool_result.title: Simulated home-charging compatibility offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical products, charging power, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added a free check of the owner's car model and home wiring with a written assurance that the set would work with both; the other listed the same compatibility tables for the owner to check. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 32 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

X1.method: Online survey with simulated product pages. Participants view two identical product descriptions of LAPP cables for home automation: one emphasizing easy installation and compatibility with popular smart home platforms (T1), the other emphasizing safety compliance and code‑meeting certification (T2). Both versions include price at 15% above standard cable price. Participants indicate which version they would choose and the
X1.sample: 500 German homeowners aged 25–55 who have installed smart home devices in their homes. Recruited via an online panel to ensure geographic coverage.
X1.measure: Purchase intent measured as binary choice between the two versions. Secondary measure: willingness to pay a premium (15% above standard price).

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 40% of participants will choose the version emphasizing installation ease and compatibility, indicating demand for a differentiated consumer proposition.
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 40% of participants will choose the version emphasizing safety compliance, indicating demand for a differentiated consumer proposition that highlights code‑meeting certification.

revisions.reason: Simulated result SYN-LAPP-UPDATE concerns compatibility uncertainty for electric-car owners purchasing home charging cables, not consumer demand for installation ease or safety compliance. It does not address T1's core premise that consumers adopt LAPP cables for home automation if the company offers a differentiated proposition emphasizing ease of installation and compatibility with smart home platforms.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed consumer preference test (X1) to validate demand for installation ease versus safety compliance before committing resources.
final.target_customer: German homeowners aged 25–55 who have installed smart home devices and are considering purchasing cables for home automation.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated consumer line of LAPP cables that emphasizes easy installation, compatibility with popular smart home platforms, and a clear safety/code‑compliance message, priced at a premium of 15% above standard cable price.
final.next_action: Run the 10‑week, €18,000 consumer preference test (X1) with 500 participants to measure purchase intent for installation‑ease versus safety‑compliance versions of the same product.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 (installation ease) and T2 (safety compliance) remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer demand and willingness to pay for these attributes.
would_change_if: If the test shows at least 40% of participants choose the version emphasizing installation ease, indicating demand for a differentiated consumer proposition.
If a separate test shows that safety‑compliance messaging drives purchase intent above 40%, shifting support to T2.

result.title: Simulated home-charging compatibility offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical products, charging power, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added a free check of the owner's car model and home wiring with a written assurance that the set would work with both; the other listed the same compatibility tables for the owner to check. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 72 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

result.title: Simulated home-charging compatibility offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical products, charging power, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added a free check of the owner's car model and home wiring with a written assurance that the set would work with both; the other listed the same compatibility tables for the owner to check. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 72 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical products, charging power, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added a free check of the owner's car model and home wiring with a written assurance that the set would work with both; the other listed the same compatibility tables for the owner to check. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 72 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

tool_result.title: Simulated household chamber-sealer running-cost offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks, hunters and anglers interested in a chamber vacuum sealer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer stated that the machine uses plain chamber pouches costing a fraction of embossed bags and showed the yearly bag cost for typical use; the other showed the same machine and listed the pouch type without a cost comparison. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 reservations for the running-cost offer and 32 for the standard offer. This tests whether running costs change choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at the machine's price, that the household market is large enough, or that it would sustain a consumer business beside the industrial one. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
tool_result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.name: WTP vs. Environmental Messaging Test
arguments.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with willingness-to-pay (WTP) and purchase intent questions.
arguments.sample: 500 German adults aged 25-55 who have purchased food in the past 12 months, recruited via an online panel.
arguments.measure: 1) Maximum price consumers would pay for a chamber sealer (WTP). 2) Purchase intent (binary: "Would you buy this product?" after price is disclosed). 3) Secondary: self-reported importance of environmental impact (1-5 scale).

prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher WTP and purchase intent among consumers who value waste reduction and cost savings. Professional-grade sealing benefits will not increase WTP.

result.title: Simulated household chamber-sealer running-cost offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks, hunters and anglers interested in a chamber vacuum sealer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer stated that the machine uses plain chamber pouches costing a fraction of embossed bags and showed the yearly bag cost for typical use; the other showed the same machine and listed the pouch type without a cost comparison. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 reservations for the running-cost offer and 32 for the standard offer. This tests whether running costs change choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at the machine's price, that the household market is large enough, or that it would sustain a consumer business beside the industrial one. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

position.recommendation: Run the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to empirically compare purchase intent and willingness to pay for sous vide‑focused versus health‑focused messaging among serious home cooks and health‑conscious consumers. If the test confirms a 5‑point difference in favor of sous vide messaging among home cooks, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting sous vide enthusiasts; otherwise, focus B

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify MULTIVAC investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B packaging and processing equipment, and identify what evidence would support that investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources; internal company data may not be available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Need to verify current reach to individual buyers and identify specific consumer use cases.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, and a viable route to market for a consumer proposition.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home food packaging, medical-grade home use, or hobbyist DIY) with a new product or service.
2) Expand the existing B2B offering by adding consumer‑friendly features or packaging solutions that can be sold through existing sales channels without a new product line.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current B2B customers and existing product portfolio.
4) Partner with or license technology to existing consumer brands or retailers to bring MULTIVAC packaging to consumers without direct consumer sales.

T1.claim: Serious home cooks and food enthusiasts will purchase MULTIVAC vacuum chamber machines for sous vide cooking and bulk food processing because they value professional-grade sealing performance and the ability to achieve airtight, mess-free results.
T1.who_benefits: Home cooks and culinary enthusiasts who prepare gourmet meals for family or friends, and who are willing to invest in premium kitchen equipment for quality control.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: These consumers prioritize food freshness and safety, and they appreciate the precision control that chamber sealers provide for temperature and pressure, enabling better outcomes for sous vide and bulk food storage.
T1.how_value_is_captured: MULTIVAC would capture value by selling direct to consumers through online channels or specialty retailers, pricing at a premium justified by performance, and earning recurring revenue from consumables (bags, accessories).
assumptions: Home vacuum sealing demand exists beyond the 30% market share of commercial users.
Consumers are willing to pay €200-€500 for a tabletop chamber sealer.
Distribution can reach this segment through e-commerce or specialty kitchen retailers.
predictions: A test offering a €350 tabletop chamber sealer to 500 serious home cooks would result in at least 10% purchase conversion.
Surveyed intent to purchase would be positively correlated with self-reported sous vide cooking frequency.
Price sensitivity would be low for this segment, with only 5% of respondents citing cost as a barrier.
T1.first_claim: Serious home cooks and food enthusiasts will purchase MULTIVAC vacuum chamber machines for sous vide cooking and bulk food processing because they value professional-grade sealing performance and the ability to achieve airtight, mess-free results.

T2.claim: Health‑conscious consumers will purchase MULTIVAC vacuum chamber machines because they trust the brand’s medical‑grade packaging for food safety, and they value the ability to preserve nutrients and reduce food waste.
T2.who_benefits: Consumers who prioritize food safety and quality, especially those with dietary restrictions or who purchase organic/non‑GMO products, and who are willing to pay a premium for certified packaging.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: These consumers seek packaging that meets or exceeds food safety standards, and they believe vacuum sealing preserves nutrients and freshness longer than other methods, reducing waste.
T2.how_value_is_captured: MULTIVAC would capture value by marketing the product as a health‑focused kitchen appliance, selling through health‑food retailers and online wellness platforms, and offering optional certifications (e.g., organic, non‑GMO) at a premium.
assumptions: There is a measurable segment of consumers who actively seek medical‑grade packaging for food.
Consumers are willing to pay €300–€500 for a tabletop chamber sealer that includes a health‑food certification.
Retail partners will allocate shelf space to a product positioned as a health‑preserving kitchen appliance.
predictions: A test offering a €400 tabletop chamber sealer to 500 health‑conscious consumers would result in at least 8% purchase conversion.
Surveyed intent to purchase would be positively correlated with self‑reported frequency of buying organic/non‑GMO produce.
Price sensitivity would be moderate, with 15% citing cost as a barrier but also 20% willing to pay a premium for certification.

result.title: Simulated household chamber-sealer running-cost offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks, hunters and anglers interested in a chamber vacuum sealer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer stated that the machine uses plain chamber pouches costing a fraction of embossed bags and showed the yearly bag cost for typical use; the other showed the same machine and listed the pouch type without a cost comparison. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 reservations for the running-cost offer and 72 for the standard offer. This tests whether running costs change choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at the machine's price, that the household market is large enough, or that it would sustain a consumer business beside the industrial one. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

tool_result.title: Simulated household chamber-sealer running-cost offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks, hunters and anglers interested in a chamber vacuum sealer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer stated that the machine uses plain chamber pouches costing a fraction of embossed bags and showed the yearly bag cost for typical use; the other showed the same machine and listed the pouch type without a cost comparison. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 reservations for the running-cost offer and 72 for the standard offer. This tests whether running costs change choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at the machine's price, that the household market is large enough, or that it would sustain a consumer business beside the industrial one. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

position.recommendation: Run the proposed Consumer Purchase Intent Test (X1) to empirically compare purchase intent and willingness to pay for performance‑focused versus retail‑focused messaging. The test will determine whether consumers respond to professional‑grade sealing performance or to retail accessibility, and will provide evidence to justify investment in a differentiated consumer proposition.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify MULTIVAC investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B packaging and processing equipment, and identify what evidence would support that investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources; internal company data may not be available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Need to verify current reach to individual buyers and identify specific consumer use cases.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, and a viable route to market for a consumer proposition.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home food packaging, medical device packaging) with a new product or service.
2) Expand the existing B2B offering by adding consumer‑friendly features or packaging solutions without creating a separate consumer brand.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current B2B packaging machines and processing equipment for food, medical, pharmaceutical, and industrial producers.
4) Partner with or license technology to existing consumer brands rather than creating a new consumer proposition.
5) Target small‑batch craft producers or hobbyists with specialized packaging solutions.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home textile spinning, hobbyist yarn production) with a new product or service.

T1.claim: Hobbyists and small-scale creators will adopt Rieter’s entry-level spinning machines because they need affordable automation to speed their creative process, and Rieter’s existing B2B reputation makes them trust the technology.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: These users value speed and consistency; they are willing to invest in a machine that reduces manual effort and increases yield, especially when the price is comparable to other hobbyist options.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Rieter captures value by selling machines under its own brand at a premium price, leveraging its existing service and support infrastructure, and potentially offering consumables or accessories.

Rieter’s B2B reputation transfers trust to consumer products.
The target market is large enough to justify a dedicated consumer line.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Rieter Holding AG investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current industrial spinning machines, components, and after-sales services.
constraints: Limited to public sources; internal financial and contractual detail may not be available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Need to discover Rieter’s current reach to individual buyers and identify a specific consumer use case with measurable demand.
Evidence must demonstrate that a consumer proposition would generate value for Rieter, not just for end‑users.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home textile spinning, hobbyist yarn production) with a new product or service.
2) Expand Rieter’s existing B2B offerings into adjacent industrial segments (e.g., specialty fibers, sustainable spinning) without creating a consumer proposition.
3) Maintain the current business model with no expansion (status quo).
4) License Rieter technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than selling under Rieter’s own brand.
5) Partner with existing consumer brands to co‑develop a consumer‑focused spinning solution.

T1.claim: Hobbyists and small-scale creators will adopt Rieter’s entry-level spinning machines because they need affordable automation to speed their creative process, and Rieter’s existing expertise in textile calculations makes the machines more appealing.
T1.who_benefits: Hobbyists, hand spinners, and small-space creators who want to produce yarn for personal projects.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: These users currently face high entry barriers (cost, learning curve) and limited options. A low‑cost, automated spinning solution would reduce time and effort, making it worthwhile to switch from manual methods.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Rieter would sell the Artisan line directly to consumers at a modest margin, leveraging its existing textile calculator brand trust to differentiate the consumer proposition.
assumptions: Hobbyists are willing to invest in equipment that reduces project time.
The market for entry‑level spinning machines exists and is large enough to justify production.
Rieter can adapt its existing technology (e.g., carding, drawing) to a consumer‑friendly package.
predictions: If offered, hobbyists will purchase the Artisan line at a rate sufficient to achieve a positive return on investment within 12 months.
Sales will be concentrated in regions with strong craft and textile communities (e.g., Europe, North America).

result.title: Simulated mini-spinning-machine onboarding offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby spinners and small fibre-farm owners interested in a compact electric spinning machine were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, output, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included two live training sessions with a spinning instructor and a setup visit; the other included the same machine with a printed manual and video links. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the instructor-onboarding offer and 32 for the manual-only offer. This tests whether the skill barrier changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a spinning-machine maker could build such a machine at a price these buyers pay, that the hobby market is large enough, or that it would fit an industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

tool_result.title: Simulated mini-spinning-machine onboarding offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby spinners and small fibre-farm owners interested in a compact electric spinning machine were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, output, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included two live training sessions with a spinning instructor and a setup visit; the other included the same machine with a printed manual and video links. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the instructor-onboarding offer and 32 for the manual-only offer. This tests whether the skill barrier changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a spinning-machine maker could build such a machine at a price these buyers pay, that the hobby market is large enough, or that it would fit an industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Rieter Holding AG investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current industrial spinning machines, components, and after-sales services.

T1.claim: Hobbyist craft yarn consumers will adopt home spinning machines if they perceive the process as creative and rewarding, and if Rieter provides a consumer-friendly, low-entry platform that integrates with existing craft communities.
T1.who_benefits: Rieter gains premium consumer revenue and brand extension; hobbyists gain a new creative outlet and access to high-quality yarn.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Crafters increasingly seek novel activities; a low-cost spinning kit that yields unique yarn aligns with their desire for personal expression and can be shared within the craft community.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Rieter sells a consumer-grade spinning kit at a modest price point, captures margin through accessories and community-driven services, and leverages its existing industrial technology to ensure consistent yarn quality.
assumptions: Craft yarn market growth continues at least 5% annually.
Hobbyists are willing to pay €200-€400 for a spinning kit that produces high-quality yarn.
Rieter can adapt its industrial machines to produce consumer-grade yarn without major redesign.
predictions: If offered, at least 1,000 units of a consumer kit will be sold within 12 weeks in a test market.
Customer satisfaction scores will be above 4.5/5, indicating perception of creativity and reward.
Repeat purchase rate for accessories and community services will exceed 30% within 6 months.

result.title: Simulated mini-spinning-machine onboarding offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby spinners and small fibre-farm owners interested in a compact electric spinning machine were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, output, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included two live training sessions with a spinning instructor and a setup visit; the other included the same machine with a printed manual and video links. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the instructor-onboarding offer and 72 for the manual-only offer. This tests whether the skill barrier changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a spinning-machine maker could build such a machine at a price these buyers pay, that the hobby market is large enough, or that it would fit an industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-RIETER-UPDATE concerns a training-inclusive offer versus a manual-only offer for hobby spinners, not the broader consumer proposition. tool_result.question: Should Rieter Holding AG develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing short-staple spinning machines, components and after-sales services for industrial spinning mills? What evidence would justify that investment?
tool_result.brief: Rieter Holding AG makes systems for short-staple fibre spinning, from fibre preparation to ring, compact, rotor and air-jet spinning and winding, together with components and after-sales services, for spinning mills; since February 2026 it also owns Barmag, a maker of man-made fibre equipment. It is a listed group headquartered in Winterthur, Switzerland, with more than 3,000 mill customers. You have not been told how far it already reaches individual buyers, so find out. You are an outside analyst working only from public sources. This company has not asked this question, has not been contacted, and nothing here describes its intentions. Some of its financial and contractual detail may not be public, so say what you could not find. Product redesign, a different route to buyers, a different customer group and no expansion are all open. The test budget of 20000 euros and the 12-week limit are analyst assumptions for this exercise, not company figures.

result.title: Simulated mini-spinning-machine onboarding offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby spinners and small fibre-farm owners interested in a compact electric spinning machine were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, output, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included two live training sessions with a spinning instructor and a setup visit; the other included the same machine with a printed manual and video links. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the instructor-onboarding offer and 72 for the manual-only offer. This tests whether the skill barrier changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a spinning-machine maker could build such a machine at a price these buyers pay, that the hobby market is large enough, or that it would fit an industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

tool_result.title: Simulated mini-spinning-machine onboarding offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby spinners and small fibre-farm owners interested in a compact electric spinning machine were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, output, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included two live training sessions with a spinning instructor and a setup visit; the other included the same machine with a printed manual and video links. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the instructor-onboarding offer and 72 for the manual-only offer. This tests whether the skill barrier changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a spinning-machine maker could build such a machine at a price these buyers pay, that the hobby market is large enough, or that it would fit an industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

frame.objective: Determine whether Kardex Holding AG should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B automated storage and retrieval systems, and identify what evidence would justify that investment.
constraints: Limited public information on Kardex’s current consumer reach and sales channels.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Need to find evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive positioning before committing resources.
Must consider manufacturing feasibility, regulatory requirements, and potential partner/channel relationships.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual homeowners or small businesses for home storage/organizing (e.g., automated garage storage, small‑scale vertical storage).
2) Expand into consumer markets with existing B2B products by offering subscription or rental models, or bundling with home‑improvement retailers.
3) No expansion – continue focusing exclusively on current B2B automated storage solutions for warehouses, factories, and organizations.
4) Partner with established consumer brands or retailers to bring Kardex technology to consumer markets without direct consumer branding.
5) Create a consumer‑focused product line for a niche use case (e.g., medical supply storage for home‑use) and sell directly to consumers online.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: When the price point aligns with existing alternatives, consumers shift from discretionary purchases to long‑term operational cost savings, making a differentiated consumer proposition economically attractive.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Kardex captures value through subscription fees, service contracts, and potential hardware sales, leveraging existing B2B service infrastructure.
assumptions: Consumers prioritize total cost of ownership over upfront price.
Alternative storage solutions are readily available and known.

predictions: If offered at a price comparable to a rented storage unit, Kardex will achieve a minimum of 5% market penetration among target households.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Cost vs Status Messaging
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.
X1.sample: 500 homeowners and small business owners in Switzerland and the US, recruited via panel, balanced for age, income, and home ownership status.
X1.measure: 1) Binary choice: "Would you purchase this system?" 2) WTP: maximum price willing to pay (EUR). 3) Additional comments on reasons for purchase.

prediction_by_theory.T1: When presented with cost-focused messaging (TCO comparison to alternative storage), at least 15% will choose to purchase and WTP will be within 10% of the baseline price (e.g., $95k).
prediction_by_theory.T2: When presented with status/lifestyle messaging (design, integration, smart home compatibility), at least 15% will choose to purchase and WTP will be at least 20% above the baseline price (e.g., $114k).

X1.decision_rule: If the choice rate for either messaging exceeds 15% and the corresponding WTP is within the predicted range, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If neither meets the threshold, recommend no expansion.

revisions.reason: Simulated result SYN-KARDEX-UPDATE shows that a monthly rental offer with no upfront payment achieved 72 letters of intent among 800 small‑business owners, while an outright purchase offer achieved only 32. This supports T1's premise that total cost of ownership (TCO) comparison influences adoption, because the rental model effectively lowers upfront cost and still generates commitment.

tool_result.title: Simulated compact storage-module payment offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small workshops, shops and garages were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact automated storage module. Both showed the identical machine, capacity, installation, service and total cost over five years. One offer was a monthly rental with service included and no upfront payment; the other was an outright purchase with the same service contract. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a signed letter of intent not withdrawn after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 letters of intent for the rental offer and 32 for the purchase offer. This tests whether the upfront cost changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a module small and cheap enough could be built, that installation and service would pay at this scale, or that private households would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
tool_result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

result.title: Simulated compact storage-module payment offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small workshops, shops and garages were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact automated storage module. Both showed the identical machine, capacity, installation, service and total cost over five years. One offer was a monthly rental with service included and no upfront payment; the other was an outright purchase with the same service contract. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a signed letter of intent not withdrawn after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 letters of intent for the rental offer and 32 for the purchase offer. This tests whether the upfront cost changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a module small and cheap enough could be built, that installation and service would pay at this scale, or that private households would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

tool_result.title: Simulated compact storage-module payment offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small workshops, shops and garages were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact automated storage module. Both showed the identical machine, capacity, installation, service and total cost over five years. One offer was a monthly rental with service included and no upfront payment; the other was an outright purchase with the same service contract. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a signed letter of intent not withdrawn after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 letters of intent for the rental offer and 32 for the purchase offer. This tests whether the upfront cost changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a module small and cheap enough could be built, that installation and service would pay at this scale, or that private households would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

frame.objective: Determine whether Kardex Holding AG should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B automated storage and retrieval systems, and identify what evidence would justify that investment.
constraints: Limited public information on Kardex’s current consumer reach and sales channels.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Need to find evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive positioning for a new consumer proposition.
Must consider manufacturing feasibility, regulatory requirements, and potential disruption to existing B2B business.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual homeowners or small businesses for home storage and organization (e.g., automated garage storage systems).
2) Expand into a new B2B segment such as retail stores or e‑commerce fulfillment centers with a customized consumer‑focused solution.
3) No expansion – continue focusing exclusively on existing B2B automated storage and retrieval systems for warehouses, factories, and organizations.
4) License Kardex’s technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than selling under Kardex’s own brand.
5) Partner with consumer retailers to co‑brand and distribute Kardex’s consumer products, leveraging existing retail channels.

T1.who_benefits: Kardex would benefit from premium pricing and brand association with modern, tech‑savvy homes.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers increasingly seek products that reflect personal style and demonstrate capability; automated storage offers convenience and a visible technological advantage.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Kardex would capture value through higher per‑unit margins, brand licensing opportunities, and recurring service contracts.
assumptions: Consumers in target segments (e.g., tech‑savvy homeowners, early adopters) value convenience and status.
Marketing can effectively communicate the product's lifestyle and technological benefits.
Distribution channels (e.g., specialty retailers, online premium marketplaces) are willing to stock and promote high‑margin consumer offerings.
predictions: Surveyed homeowners will indicate willingness to pay a premium (e.g., 20% above standard storage solutions) for automated home storage.
Sales in premium segments will grow faster than overall revenue, indicating consumer adoption.
Brand perception surveys will show association of Kardex with modern, tech‑forward homes.

assumptions: Homeowners face storage constraints that cannot be addressed by existing solutions.
Convenience and ease of use are primary purchase drivers.
Price sensitivity is moderate; a modest premium is acceptable if it delivers measurable space gains.
predictions: Surveyed homeowners will indicate willingness to purchase automated storage if it provides at least 20% more usable space compared to standard solutions.

X1.name: Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Automated Home Storage
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants view a product description emphasizing either status/modern lifestyle (T1) or functional storage gain (T2). They are asked: "How much would you pay for a Kardex automated home storage system that meets the following description?" They can select a price range (e.g., $1,000–$5,000) and indicate which description they find more important. The survey also collects demographic data (age, income, home ownership status).
X1.sample: 500 homeowners in the United States, recruited via an online panel, balanced across age groups and income brackets.
X1.measure: Average price selected for the status‑focused description versus the functional‑storage description, and the percentage of participants who select a price above $2,000 (a threshold reflecting a premium).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Average price for status‑focused description will be at least 20% higher than for functional‑storage description, and at least 30% of participants will select a price above $2,000.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Average price for functional‑storage description will be at least 20% higher than for status‑focused description, and at least 30% of participants will select a price above $2,000.

X1.decision_rule: If the average price for status‑focused description exceeds the functional‑storage description by ≥ 20% AND at least 30% of participants select a price above $2,000, then T1 is supported. If the opposite pattern occurs, T2 is supported. If neither condition is met, both theories remain uncertain.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-KARDEX-UPDATE concerns a rental versus purchase choice for a compact automated storage module, not consumer demand drivers. It does not address status/modern lifestyle messaging (T1) or functional storage gain (T2). Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

result.title: Simulated compact storage-module payment offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small workshops, shops and garages were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact automated storage module. Both showed the identical machine, capacity, installation, service and total cost over five years. One offer was a monthly rental with service included and no upfront payment; the other was an outright purchase with the same service contract. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a signed letter of intent not withdrawn after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 letters of intent for the rental offer and 72 for the purchase offer. This tests whether the upfront cost changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a module small and cheap enough could be built, that installation and service would pay at this scale, or that private households would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. frame.objective: Determine whether Kardex Holding AG should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B automated storage and retrieval systems, and identify what evidence would justify that investment.
constraints: Limited public information on Kardex’s current consumer reach and sales channels.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Need to find evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive positioning for a consumer proposition.
Must consider manufacturing feasibility, regulatory requirements, and potential cannibalization of existing B2B markets.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual homeowners or small businesses for home storage and organization (e.g., automated garage storage systems).
2) Expand into a new B2B segment such as retail stores or e‑commerce fulfillment centers with a customized consumer‑focused solution.
3) No expansion – continue focusing exclusively on existing B2B automated storage and retrieval systems for warehouses, factories, and organizations.
4) License Kardex’s technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than selling under Kardex’s own brand.
5) Partner with consumer retailers to co‑brand and distribute Kardex’s consumer products, leveraging existing retail channels.

T1.claim: Homeowners will adopt automated storage systems if they perceive a clear functional benefit (e.g., increased space efficiency) and can afford the price, because they value convenience and reduced manual effort.
T1.who_benefits: Individual homeowners seeking to maximize storage capacity in limited space.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: When homeowners experience a measurable reduction in time spent organizing and retrieving items, and when the price aligns with their willingness to pay for a solution that solves a pressing problem, they will switch from manual to
T1.how_value_is_captured: Kardex can capture value by selling the system under its own brand, leveraging its existing distribution channels, and potentially offering subscription services for maintenance and upgrades.
assumptions: Homeowners are aware of Kardex’s consumer products and understand their benefits.
Price sensitivity is such that a premium for automation is acceptable for a significant portion of homeowners.
There is sufficient unmet demand for home storage solutions to justify a new consumer proposition.
predictions: If offered a Kardex automated garage storage system, at least 15% of surveyed homeowners will express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.
Purchase intent will be positively correlated with perceived functional benefit (e.g., increased usable space) and affordability relative to alternative solutions.
T1.first_claim: Homeowners will adopt automated storage systems if they perceive a clear functional benefit (e.g., increased space efficiency) and can afford the price, because they value convenience and reduced manual effort.

T2.claim: Small businesses and startups will adopt automated storage systems if they reduce overhead costs and increase operational efficiency, because they prioritize cost-effective solutions that maximize productivity.

result.title: Simulated compact storage-module payment offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small workshops, shops and garages were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact automated storage module. Both showed the identical machine, capacity, installation, service and total cost over five years. One offer was a monthly rental with service included and no upfront payment; the other was an outright purchase with the same service contract. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a signed letter of intent not withdrawn after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 letters of intent for the rental offer and 72 for the purchase offer. This tests whether the upfront cost changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a module small and cheap enough could be built, that installation and service would pay at this scale, or that private households would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

tool_result.title: Simulated compact storage-module payment offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small workshops, shops and garages were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact automated storage module. Both showed the identical machine, capacity, installation, service and total cost over five years. One offer was a monthly rental with service included and no upfront payment; the other was an outright purchase with the same service contract. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a signed letter of intent not withdrawn after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 letters of intent for the rental offer and 72 for the purchase offer. This tests whether the upfront cost changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a module small and cheap enough could be built, that installation and service would pay at this scale, or that private households would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

X1.name: Retail vs Contractor Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants view a product description for a Sika sealant (specifying DIY use) and are asked: "Which channel would you buy this product through?" (A) Retail partner (hardware store), (B) Contractor/distributor, (C) Direct from Sika. They also indicate willingness to pay a premium price (e.g., 20% above standard retail price).
X1.sample: 500 DIY consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and home improvement experience.
X1.measure: Proportion of participants choosing channel A (retail) vs channel B (contractor/distributor). Secondary measure: average premium price willingness.

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 60% of participants will select channel A (retail) and indicate willingness to pay a premium price comparable to standard retail margins.
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 60% of participants will select channel B (contractor/distributor) and indicate willingness to pay a premium price comparable to B2B margins.

X1.decision_rule: If the proportion choosing channel A is at least 10 percentage points higher than channel B, T1 is favoured. If channel B is at least 10 percentage points higher, T2 is favoured. If the difference is <10 percentage points, both theories remain uncertain.

revisions.reason: Simulated result SYN-SIKA-UPDATE concerns a test of application-kit versus cartridge-only sealant offers, not consumer purchase channels. It does not address whether consumers buy Sika through retail partners or contractors/distributors, so it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

final.recommendation: Run the proposed Retail vs Contractor Messaging Test (X1) to measure consumer channel preference and willingness to pay. If the test shows at least a 10-percentage-point advantage for retail (channel A) over contractor/distributor (channel B), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for retail distribution. If the test shows no clear advantage, maintain the current B2B focus. The test cost is €15,000

final.next_action: Execute the Retail vs Contractor Messaging Test (X1) within 12 weeks, recruiting 500 DIY consumers and measuring channel preference and willingness to pay.
final.uncertainty: Both theories remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer purchase channels and willingness to pay for retail versus contractor pricing.
would_change_if: If the test shows a ≥10-percentage-point advantage for retail (channel A) over contractor/distributor (channel B), indicating consumer preference for retail distribution.
If the test shows no clear advantage, indicating that consumers remain reliant on professional channels and that a consumer proposition would not drive demand.

arguments.name: Retail vs Contractor Messaging Test
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants view a product description for a Sika sealant (specifying DIY use) and are asked: "Which channel would you buy this product through?" (A) Retail partner (hardware store), (B) Contractor/distributor, (C) Direct from Sika. They also indicate willingness to pay a premium price (e.g., 20% above standard retail price).
arguments.sample: 500 DIY consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and home improvement experience.
arguments.measure: Proportion of participants choosing channel A (retail) vs channel B (contractor/distributor). Secondary measure: average premium price willingness.

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 60% of participants will select channel A (retail) and indicate willingness to pay a premium price comparable to standard retail margins.
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 60% of participants will select channel B (contractor/distributor) and indicate willingness to pay a premium price comparable to B2B margins.

arguments.decision_rule: If the proportion choosing channel A is at least 10 percentage points higher than channel B, T1 is favoured. If channel B is at least 10 percentage points higher, T2 is favoured. If the difference is <10 percentage points, both theories remain uncertain.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Run the proposed Retail vs Contractor Messaging Test (X1) to measure consumer channel preference and willingness to pay. If the test shows at least a 10-percentage-point advantage for retail (channel A) over contractor/distributor (channel B), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for retail distribution. If the test shows no clear advantage, maintain the current B2B focus. The test cost is €15,000

arguments.who_benefits: DIY homeowners and small contractors who need reliable products for everyday projects.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: If consumers believe Sika’s DIY products deliver professional results, they will purchase them instead of cheaper alternatives, even at higher prices, because they value quality and reliability.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Sika can charge premium prices for branded DIY products and sell through retail channels, capturing value through brand trust and consistent performance.

predictions: In a test offering a Sika DIY sealant at a price 15% above competitors, purchase intent among DIY shoppers will be at least 10 percentage points higher than for a generic sealant.

arguments.why_behaviour_changes: If consumers can buy Sika DIY products online, they will choose them over competitors that require in‑store visits, because online shopping eliminates travel time, reduces search effort, and offers price transparency.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Sika can capture value through online sales commissions, higher per‑unit margins, and brand exposure in digital marketplaces, while leveraging existing distribution networks to reach consumers.
assumptions: Consumers prioritize convenience and speed in purchasing building supplies.
Online marketplaces have sufficient reach to Sika’s target DIY audience.
Sika can maintain brand perception and product quality in digital channels.
predictions: In a test offering Sika DIY sealant exclusively online at the same price as a comparable brand sold in stores, purchase intent among online shoppers will be at least 15 percentage points higher than for the same product sold only in stores.

result.title: Simulated home-sealant application offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home owners planning to reseal a bathroom or window were assigned equally to two offers for the same sealant. Both showed the identical product, colour range, cure time, price, shelf life and return policy. One offer was a kit with a smoothing tool, masking tape and a step-by-step guide for a clean finish; the other was the same cartridge with the standard label instructions. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the application-kit offer and 32 for the cartridge-only offer. This tests whether application difficulty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the margin on a kit, how retailers would stock it, or that DIY volumes would matter beside professional sales. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
