frame.objective: Determine whether Sika AG should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B construction chemicals, sealants, and adhesives, and identify what evidence would justify that investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources; internal company data may not be available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Need to discover Sika’s current reach to individual buyers and any existing consumer products.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, and a viable route to consumers for a new proposition.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., DIY waterproofing, home flooring bonding) with a new product and direct-to-consumer sales channel.
2) Expand existing B2B offerings into new consumer segments via existing distribution (e.g., offering contractor‑grade products to homeowners through retail partners).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current B2B construction chemicals, sealants, and adhesives without adding consumer propositions.

T1.claim: Consumers purchase Sika DIY products primarily for quick, reliable performance in everyday home repair and improvement, valuing professional-grade results and ease of use over price.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners and DIY enthusiasts who need functional solutions for common building tasks.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If consumers perceive a product as delivering consistent professional results that save time and reduce rework, they will choose it over cheaper alternatives, even if it is marketed as a premium brand.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Sika can charge premium prices for products that meet or exceed DIY expectations, and can expand its consumer presence by leveraging existing retail channels (e.g., hardware stores, online marketplaces) without major new manufacturing.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for products they trust will perform as advertised.
Retail partners will stock Sika products if they meet DIY demand and pricing.
Marketing can communicate professional-grade performance effectively to DIY buyers.
predictions: In a test offering a premium-priced sealant marketed for DIY waterproofing, purchase intent will be higher than for a similarly priced generic alternative.
Surveyed DIY buyers will cite performance reliability and ease of use as top purchase drivers.

result.title: Simulated home-sealant application offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home owners planning to reseal a bathroom or window were assigned equally to two offers for the same sealant. Both showed the identical product, colour range, cure time, price, shelf life and return policy. One offer was a kit with a smoothing tool, masking tape and a step-by-step guide for a clean finish; the other was the same cartridge with the standard label instructions. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the application-kit offer and 72 for the cartridge-only offer. This tests whether application difficulty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the margin on a kit, how retailers would stock it, or that DIY volumes would matter beside professional sales. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

position.recommendation: Run the proposed DIY Sealant Choice Test (X1) to empirically compare consumer choice at a 15% premium (performance trust) versus a 10% premium (convenience/brand trust). The test will decide whether to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, focusing on performance if the 15% premium share meets the decision threshold, or explore other options if the test results do not support T1.

frame.objective: Determine whether Sika AG should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B construction chemicals, sealants, and adhesives, and identify what evidence would justify that investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources; internal company data may not be available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Need to discover Sika’s current reach to individual buyers and any existing consumer products.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, and a viable route to consumers for a new proposition.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., DIY waterproofing, home flooring bonding) with a new product and direct-to-consumer sales channel.
2) Expand existing B2B offerings into new consumer segments via existing distribution (e.g., offering contractor‑grade products to homeowners through retail partners).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current B2B construction chemicals, sealants, and adhesives without adding consumer propositions.

T1.claim: Consumers will purchase Sika’s construction sealants and adhesives for DIY projects when they perceive clear performance benefits (professional results, durability, safety) and can easily find the products through existing retail channels (e.g., Amazon, home improvement stores).
T1.who_benefits: DIY homeowners seeking reliable, safe products for home improvement.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If consumers trust Sika’s professional reputation and find the products readily available, they will choose them over competitors, even at higher price, because they expect superior performance.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Sika can charge premium prices for trusted DIY products and earn recurring revenue through repeat purchases of the same brand.
assumptions: DIY consumers prioritize performance over cost for safety-critical applications.
Existing retail distribution (e.g., Amazon, Home Depot) reaches DIY buyers effectively.
Sika can communicate performance claims clearly to DIY buyers.
predictions: In a test offering a Sika DIY sealant at a price 15% above competitors in a major retailer, DIY buyers will select it over competitors in >40% of purchases.
Purchase intent surveys will show >55% of DIY respondents would buy Sika for a home improvement project if they found it in a familiar retailer.
Customer reviews of Sika DIY products will highlight performance and safety benefits, reinforcing trust.
T1.first_claim: Consumers will purchase Sika’s construction sealants and adhesives for DIY projects when they perceive clear performance benefits (professional results, durability, safety) and can easily find the products through existing retail channels (e.g., Amazon, home improvement stores).

T2.claim: Consumers will purchase Sika’s construction sealants and adhesives for DIY projects when they seek convenience and trust the brand’s reputation for quality, leading them to choose Sika over competitors even if the price is modestly higher.
T2.who_benefits: DIY homeowners who value time-saving, reliable products and are willing to pay a premium for brand trust.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Convenience (one-stop shopping, easy online ordering) and brand trust (Sika’s professional reputation) reduce the perceived risk of choosing an unfamiliar product, causing consumers to select Sika even when alternatives are available.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Sika can charge a modest premium for convenience and brand trust, generating higher average order value and repeat purchases through its existing retail channels.
assumptions: DIY consumers prioritize convenience and brand reputation over price for essential building products.
Sika’s presence in major retailers (e.g., Amazon, Home Depot) provides perceived convenience.
Brand trust is transferred from professional construction applications to consumer DIY projects.
predictions: In a test offering a Sika DIY sealant at a price 10% above competitors in a major retailer, DIY buyers will select it in >35% of purchases when convenience and brand trust are highlighted.
Purchase intent surveys will show >50% of DIY respondents would buy Sika for a home improvement project if they find it in a familiar retailer that offers easy online ordering.
Customer reviews will emphasize convenience and brand reputation as key purchase drivers.

X1.method: Online choice experiment with simulated purchase scenario.
X1.sample: 500 DIY homeowners recruited via panel, balanced for age, gender, and home improvement experience.
X1.measure: Percentage of participants who select Sika DIY sealant over a competitor at a 15% price premium (T1) and at a 10% price premium (T2). Secondary measure: stated willingness to pay (WTP) on a 7-point scale.

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 40% will choose Sika at the 15% premium, indicating performance trust drives purchase.
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 35% will choose Sika at the 10% premium, indicating convenience and brand trust drive purchase.

X1.decision_rule: If Sika’s choice share at the 15% premium ≥ 40% and its choice share at the 10% premium ≤ 35%, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition focused on performance (T1). If Sika’s choice share at the 10% premium ≥ 35% and its choice share at the 15% premium ≤ 30

revisions.reason: Simulated result SYN-SIKA-UPDATE concerns a test of a DIY sealant kit versus a standard cartridge, measuring purchase choice. It does not address consumer willingness to pay a premium for performance trust, which is the core mechanism of T1. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

final.recommendation: Run the proposed DIY Sealant Choice Test (X1) to empirically compare consumer choice at a 15% premium (performance trust) versus a 10% premium (convenience/brand trust). The test will decide whether to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, focusing on performance if the 15% premium share meets the decision threshold, or explore other options if the test results do not support T1.
final.target_customer: DIY homeowners who engage in home improvement projects and seek reliable, professional-grade sealants and adhesives.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated consumer line of Sika DIY sealants that emphasizes superior performance and professional trust, sold through existing retail channels (e.g., Amazon, Home Depot) at a modest premium, delivering safety and durability benefits
final.next_action: Execute the 10‑week, €18,000 online choice experiment with 500 DIY homeowners, measuring choice at 15% and 10% price premiums. Analyze results against the decision threshold to decide whether to proceed with a consumer proposition.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 (performance trust) and T2 (convenience/brand trust) remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer willingness to pay a premium for either mechanism. The test will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows <40% choose Sika at the 15% premium, indicating performance trust is insufficient, the recommendation would shift toward exploring other consumer options or no expansion.
If the test shows >35% choose Sika at the 10% premium, indicating convenience/brand trust drives purchase, the recommendation would favor a convenience‑focused proposition.

In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home owners planning to reseal a bathroom or window were assigned equally to two offers for the same sealant. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the application-kit offer and 72 for the cartridge-only offer. This tests whether application difficulty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the margin on a kit, how retailers would stock it, or that DIY volumes would matter beside professional sales. tool_result.title: Simulated home container-collection offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited households in a deposit-return scheme were assigned equally to two offers for returning empty containers. Both paid the identical deposit refund into the same app, with the same fee and payout time. One offer collected bagged containers from the household's door every two weeks; the other asked the household to drop the same bags at a return point in a nearby store. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a bonus. The outcome was a paid sign-up still active after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 active sign-ups for the doorstep-collection offer and 32 for the store drop-off offer. This tests whether the return trip changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that collection could be run at that fee, how store partners would respond, or that households would pay for anything beyond the refund. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

X1.name: Digital Refund vs Subscription Refund Pilot
X1.method: Randomized controlled trial with two parallel groups in two pilot regions. Group A receives a consumer reverse vending machine with immediate digital refund via a mobile app; Group B receives the same machine but with a subscription refund model (monthly credit for recycled weight). Both groups are offered the same machine at no upfront cost and are tracked for container return rates over 12 weeks.
X1.sample: 200 households in each pilot region (total 400 households), recruited via local recycling programs and community outreach. Each household receives a unique code to access the app and track refunds.
X1.measure: Primary outcome: container return rate per household per week (measured via machine sensor and app data). Secondary outcomes: average refund amount per household, subscription uptake rate (for Group B), and self‑reported willingness to pay for the service.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will show a return rate at least 20% higher than Group B, because the digital refund removes barriers and provides immediate economic value.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will show a return rate at least 30% higher than Group A, because the subscription refund removes upfront cost and provides a recurring incentive for continued recycling.

Therefore it does not address T1, which predicts consumer adoption of a digital refund model. The evidence remains neutral for T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Conduct a low‑cost pilot test (as proposed) to compare digital refund vs subscription refund models. The pilot will provide real‑world evidence on consumer behavior and willingness to pay, allowing a data‑driven decision before any larger investment.
final.target_customer: Individual households in regions with established deposit‑return programs who currently face challenges returning containers (distance, time).
final.value_proposition: A consumer‑facing reverse vending machine that offers immediate digital refunds via a mobile app, removing the need for transport and providing tangible economic value.
final.next_action: Run the proposed 12‑week pilot with 400 households in two regions, tracking container return rates, refund amounts, and willingness to pay. Use the decision rule to determine which model is better supported.
final.uncertainty: Both models remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer adoption and willingness to pay. The pilot will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the pilot shows Group A (digital refund) achieving a return rate at least 20% higher than Group B (subscription refund), we would favor T1 and proceed to scale the digital refund model.
If Group B achieves a return rate at least 30% higher, we would favor T2 and explore subscription refunds.
If neither difference meets the 10‑percentage‑point threshold, we would conclude insufficient evidence and recommend no expansion.

result.title: Simulated home container-collection offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited households in a deposit-return scheme were assigned equally to two offers for returning empty containers. Both paid the identical deposit refund into the same app, with the same fee and payout time. One offer collected bagged containers from the household's door every two weeks; the other asked the household to drop the same bags at a return point in a nearby store. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a bonus. The outcome was a paid sign-up still active after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 active sign-ups for the doorstep-collection offer and 72 for the store drop-off offer. This tests whether the return trip changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that collection could be run at that fee, how store partners would respond, or that households would pay for anything beyond the refund. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

tool_result.title: Simulated home container-collection offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited households in a deposit-return scheme were assigned equally to two offers for returning empty containers. Both paid the identical deposit refund into the same app, with the same fee and payout time. One offer collected bagged containers from the household's door every two weeks; the other asked the household to drop the same bags at a return point in a nearby store. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a bonus. The outcome was a paid sign-up still active after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 active sign-ups for the doorstep-collection offer and 72 for the store drop-off offer. This tests whether the return trip changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that collection could be run at that fee, how store partners would respond, or that households would pay for anything beyond the refund. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

result.title: Simulated home container-collection offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited households in a deposit-return scheme were assigned equally to two offers for returning empty containers. Both paid the identical deposit refund into the same app, with the same fee and payout time. One offer collected bagged containers from the household's door every two weeks; the other asked the household to drop the same bags at a return point in a nearby store. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a bonus. The outcome was a paid sign-up still active after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 active sign-ups for the doorstep-collection offer and 72 for the store drop-off offer. This tests whether the return trip changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that collection could be run at that fee, how store partners would respond, or that households would pay for anything beyond the refund. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Brembo investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B and aftermarket offerings, and identify what evidence would support that investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources; financial and contractual detail may not be available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Need to discover Brembo’s current reach to individual buyers and any existing consumer products.
Evidence must address demand, willingness to pay, competitive landscape, and feasibility of a new consumer proposition.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., high‑performance motorcycle brakes sold directly to enthusiasts).
2) Expand into a new consumer segment without differentiation (e.g., sell existing aftermarket parts through new retail channels).
3) No expansion – maintain current B2B and aftermarket focus.
4) License Brembo’s technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than selling under its own brand.
5) Partner with established consumer brands to co‑brand a limited‑edition consumer product.

T1.who_benefits: Consumers seeking superior braking performance and a brand experience; Brembo benefits from premium pricing and brand loyalty.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: These consumers prioritize performance and differentiate themselves through top‑tier equipment; they are willing to pay more for proven motorsport technology and a brand story.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Brembo captures value through premium pricing, limited‑edition or co‑branded offerings, and potentially higher margins than standard aftermarket parts.
assumptions: Performance‑focused consumers exist in sufficient size to justify dedicated consumer lines.
Brand heritage and motorsport association are meaningful to purchase decisions.
Direct‑to‑consumer channels or limited‑edition partnerships can reach this segment.
predictions: Willingness to pay at least 20% above standard aftermarket prices for a differentiated product.
Purchase intent driven by a perceived difference in performance or brand story.
Repeat purchase rate higher than standard parts due to perceived quality and exclusivity.

T2.why_behaviour_changes: These consumers use automotive and motorcycle gear as a way to demonstrate their affiliation with a premium brand and their understanding of advanced technology; they are willing to pay more for products that signal expertise.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Brembo captures value through premium pricing, limited‑edition or co‑branded offerings, and by leveraging the brand’s reputation to command higher prices.

Direct‑to‑consumer or limited‑edition channels can reach this segment.

result.title: Simulated bicycle-brake trial offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited mountain-bike and e-bike riders considering a premium brake upgrade were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical brake kit, specifications, price, fitting service, warranty and delivery time. One offer included a free demo ride on a bike fitted with the brakes at a partner shop before ordering; the other showed the same kit with test reports and specification sheets. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the demo-ride offer and 32 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether trying the product first changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, the cost of running demo rides, or how established bicycle-brake brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Brembo investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B and aftermarket offerings, and identify what evidence would support that investment.

X1.name: Targeted Digital Campaign for Enthusiast vs Lifestyle Segments
X1.method: Run two parallel targeted digital campaigns for 12 weeks: (1) Enthusiast campaign (e.g., mountain bikers and track day drivers) featuring a premium enthusiast brake kit (e.g., GR-PRO or GT kit) sold directly at €750; (2) Lifestyle campaign (e.g., urban commuters and everyday riders) featuring the XTRA Signature disc kit (e.g., €300–400) sold directly. Both campaigns use identical landing pages with the same product description, price, and call‑to‑action ("Buy now").
X1.sample: Each campaign targets 5,000 users per segment via social media (Facebook/Instagram) and search ads (Google Ads). This yields a total of 10,000 impressions per segment.
X1.measure: Conversion rate (percentage of users who click "Buy now" and complete a purchase) and total revenue generated per segment.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Enthusiast campaign conversion rate ≥ 5% and revenue ≥ €3,750; Lifestyle campaign conversion rate < 2% and revenue < €1,200.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Lifestyle campaign conversion rate ≥ 5% and revenue ≥ €12,000; Enthusiast campaign conversion rate < 2% and revenue < €1,200.

X1.decision_rule: If either campaign meets its respective conversion/revenue threshold, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for that segment. If neither meets its threshold, conclude that there is insufficient public evidence to justify a new consumer proposition.

result.title: Simulated bicycle-brake trial offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited mountain-bike and e-bike riders considering a premium brake upgrade were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical brake kit, specifications, price, fitting service, warranty and delivery time. One offer included a free demo ride on a bike fitted with the brakes at a partner shop before ordering; the other showed the same kit with test reports and specification sheets. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the demo-ride offer and 72 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether trying the product first changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, the cost of running demo rides, or how established bicycle-brake brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited mountain-bike and e-bike riders considering a premium brake upgrade were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical brake kit, specifications, price, fitting service, warranty and delivery time. One offer included a free demo ride on a bike fitted with the brakes at a partner shop before ordering; the other showed the same kit with test reports and specification sheets. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the demo-ride offer and 72 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether trying the product first changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, the cost of running demo rides, or how established bicycle-brake brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

position.recommendation: Invest in a limited pilot of a differentiated consumer proposition targeting high‑performance motorcycle enthusiasts, using the proposed willingness‑to‑pay survey to validate demand before scaling. If the survey meets the 40% threshold for willingness to pay €750, proceed to develop a premium‑branded brake kit for enthusiasts; otherwise, abandon the consumer expansion and focus on existing B2B and aftermarket sales.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Brembo investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B and aftermarket offerings, and identify what evidence would support that investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources; financial and contractual detail may not be available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Need to discover Brembo’s current reach to individual buyers and any existing consumer products.
Evidence must address demand, willingness to pay, competitive landscape, and feasibility of a new consumer proposition.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., high‑performance motorcycle brakes sold directly to enthusiasts).
2) Expand into a new consumer segment without differentiation (e.g., sell existing aftermarket parts through new retail channels).
3) No expansion – maintain current B2B and aftermarket focus.
4) License Brembo’s technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than selling under its own brand.
5) Partner with established consumer brands to co‑brand a limited‑edition consumer product.

T1.claim: High‑performance motorcycle enthusiasts will purchase Brembo’s premium brake kits directly, justifying a differentiated consumer proposition.
T1.who_benefits: Enthusiast riders who value performance and exclusivity and are willing to pay premium prices for top‑tier components.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: These riders seek to maximize bike performance and status; they research and trust Brembo’s motorsport heritage and adjustability, making them less price‑sensitive to a €750 kit.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Brembo captures value through premium pricing, direct‑to‑consumer sales, and brand extension into lifestyle products, leveraging its existing aftermarket presence.
assumptions: Enthusiast riders have sufficient disposable income to afford €750 brake kits.
They actively seek out and research high‑performance brakes.
They trust Brembo’s motorsport pedigree and adjustability as a performance signal.
predictions: Surveyed enthusiasts will indicate willingness to pay €750 for a Brembo brake kit.
Sales of the kit will be concentrated among high‑income, performance‑oriented buyers.
Brand awareness among enthusiasts will increase when the kit is marketed as a premium, performance‑enhancing component.

tool_result.title: Simulated bicycle-brake trial offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited mountain-bike and e-bike riders considering a premium brake upgrade were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical brake kit, specifications, price, fitting service, warranty and delivery time. One offer included a free demo ride on a bike fitted with the brakes at a partner shop before ordering; the other showed the same kit with test reports and specification sheets. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the demo-ride offer and 72 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether trying the product first changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, the cost of running demo rides, or how established bicycle-brake brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

result.title: Simulated small-workshop CNC software offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small carpentry workshops and skilled hobby woodworkers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact CNC router. Both showed the identical machine, working area, price, installation, warranty and delivery time. One offer came with simplified design software and a library of ready-to-cut furniture templates that need no programming; the other came with the standard professional CAD/CAM software. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the template-software offer and 32 for the standard-software offer. This tests whether programming complexity changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a machine at a price these buyers pay could be built, that the market is large enough, or that it fits the company's industrial dealers. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

tool_result.title: Simulated small-workshop CNC software offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small carpentry workshops and skilled hobby woodworkers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact CNC router. Both showed the identical machine, working area, price, installation, warranty and delivery time. One offer came with simplified design software and a library of ready-to-cut furniture templates that need no programming; the other came with the standard professional CAD/CAM software. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the template-software offer and 32 for the standard-software offer. This tests whether programming complexity changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a machine at a price these buyers pay could be built, that the market is large enough, or that it fits the company's industrial dealers. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
tool_result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

frame.objective: Determine whether Biesse S.p.A. should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B offerings, based on evidence of market demand, competitive landscape, and feasibility within the analyst’s test budget and 12‑week timeframe.
constraints: Limited to public sources; financial and contractual detail may not be available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Need to verify current reach to individual buyers and identify specific use cases with measurable demand.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, and a viable route to consumers, not just product capability.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home DIY wood processing) with a new product or service.
2) Expand existing B2B offerings into new segments or markets without creating a consumer proposition (e.g., deeper penetration of construction or automotive sectors).
3) No expansion: maintain current product portfolio and distribution channels, focusing resources on existing B2B customers.

T1.claim: Homeowners will adopt Biesse CNC machines for DIY wood processing if they perceive the technology as a status symbol and a way to produce high‑quality, custom‑finished products that cannot be obtained through standard retail channels.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners seeking premium, handcrafted wood products; Biesse benefits by selling higher‑margin machines and service contracts.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If homeowners view CNC as a tool that enables them to create unique, professional‑grade items, they will be willing to invest in a machine and the associated expertise, even at a premium price.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Biesse captures value through premium pricing of machines, service contracts, and optional add‑ons; it also benefits from brand association with high‑end craftsmanship.
assumptions: Homeowners have sufficient disposable income to afford a Biesse CNC machine.
There is a market segment of hobbyists and small‑scale woodworkers willing to pay for professional‑grade results.
Biesse can communicate the status and craftsmanship benefits effectively to this segment.
predictions: Surveyed homeowners will indicate intent to purchase a Biesse CNC machine if presented with a description emphasizing status and custom‑product capabilities.
Sales of Biesse machines to individual buyers will correlate with marketing campaigns that highlight the machine’s role in creating distinctive, handcrafted items.

final.next_action: Execute the Homeowner Survey Test (X1) within the 12‑week, €20,000 budget window.

would_change_if: If the survey shows the precision‑focused description generates higher purchase intent than the status description by at least 1.5 points, we would shift focus to developing a precision‑driven consumer proposition.

result.title: Simulated small-workshop CNC software offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small carpentry workshops and skilled hobby woodworkers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact CNC router. Both showed the identical machine, working area, price, installation, warranty and delivery time. One offer came with simplified design software and a library of ready-to-cut furniture templates that need no programming; the other came with the standard professional CAD/CAM software. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the template-software offer and 32 for the standard-software offer. This tests whether programming complexity changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a machine at a price these buyers pay could be built, that the market is large enough, or that it fits the company's industrial dealers. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the template-software offer and 72 for the standard-software offer. This tests whether programming complexity changes choice in that recruited group. result.title: Simulated small-workshop CNC software offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small carpentry workshops and skilled hobby woodworkers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact CNC router. Both showed the identical machine, working area, price, installation, warranty and delivery time. One offer came with simplified design software and a library of ready-to-cut furniture templates that need no programming; the other came with the standard professional CAD/CAM software. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the template-software offer and 72 for the standard-software offer. This tests whether programming complexity changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a machine at a price these buyers pay could be built, that the market is large enough, or that it fits the company's industrial dealers. frame.objective: Determine whether Nabtesco Corporation should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B product portfolio, and identify evidence that would justify such an investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources; internal financial and contractual detail may not be available.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home automation, medical equipment, or consumer robotics) with a new product or service.

In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited older home owners and family members considering an automatic opener for a home entrance door were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical opener, installation, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added an independent safety certificate for the door's anti-pinch sensors and an in-home demonstration of the door stopping on contact; the other showed the same opener with its specification sheet. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the safety-assurance offer and 32 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether safety assurance changes choice in that recruited group. tool_result.title: Simulated home automatic-door safety offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited older home owners and family members considering an automatic opener for a home entrance door were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical opener, installation, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added an independent safety certificate for the door's anti-pinch sensors and an in-home demonstration of the door stopping on contact; the other showed the same opener with its specification sheet. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the safety-assurance offer and 32 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether safety assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, that installers would carry the product, or why a rival's home opener left the market. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
tool_result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

result.title: Simulated home automatic-door safety offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited older home owners and family members considering an automatic opener for a home entrance door were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical opener, installation, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added an independent safety certificate for the door's anti-pinch sensors and an in-home demonstration of the door stopping on contact; the other showed the same opener with its specification sheet. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the safety-assurance offer and 32 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether safety assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, that installers would carry the product, or why a rival's home opener left the market. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

tool_result.title: Simulated home automatic-door safety offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited older home owners and family members considering an automatic opener for a home entrance door were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical opener, installation, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added an independent safety certificate for the door's anti-pinch sensors and an in-home demonstration of the door stopping on contact; the other showed the same opener with its specification sheet. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the safety-assurance offer and 32 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether safety assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, that installers would carry the product, or why a rival's home opener left the market. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
tool_result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home automation, medical equipment, or consumer robotics) with a new product or service.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Medical vs Smart Home Device
X1.method: Online choice experiment with simulated product descriptions and pricing. Participants view a description of a home rehabilitation device (medical focus) and a description of a smart‑home compatible rehabilitation device (convenience focus). They are asked to indicate purchase intent on a 1‑10 scale and willingness to pay (EUR).
X1.sample: 500 adults aged 30‑65 who own a smartphone and live in a market where Nabtesco has a presence (e.g., Japan, Europe). Recruited via an online panel to ensure geographic diversity.
X1.measure: Average purchase intent score for medical device vs smart‑home device; average willingness to pay for each device.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Average purchase intent for medical device will be at least 10 points higher than for smart‑home device.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Average purchase intent for smart‑home device will be at least 10 points higher than for medical device.

X1.decision_rule: If the difference in average purchase intent between the two devices exceeds 10 points, the theory that predicts the higher intent for that device is supported. If the difference is less than 10 points, both theories remain uncertain.

result.title: Simulated home automatic-door safety offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited older home owners and family members considering an automatic opener for a home entrance door were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical opener, installation, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added an independent safety certificate for the door's anti-pinch sensors and an in-home demonstration of the door stopping on contact; the other showed the same opener with its specification sheet. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the safety-assurance offer and 72 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether safety assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, that installers would carry the product, or why a rival's home opener left the market. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

result.title: Simulated home automatic-door safety offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited older home owners and family members considering an automatic opener for a home entrance door were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical opener, installation, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added an independent safety certificate for the door's anti-pinch sensors and an in-home demonstration of the door stopping on contact; the other showed the same opener with its specification sheet. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the safety-assurance offer and 72 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether safety assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, that installers would carry the product, or why a rival's home opener left the market. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: Simulated result SYN-NABTESCO-UPDATE concerns a safety-assurance offer for automatic door openers, not home automation products. tool_result.title: Simulated home automatic-door safety offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited older home owners and family members considering an automatic opener for a home entrance door were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical opener, installation, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added an independent safety certificate for the door's anti-pinch sensors and an in-home demonstration of the door stopping on contact; the other showed the same opener with its specification sheet. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the safety-assurance offer and 72 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether safety assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, that installers would carry the product, or why a rival's home opener left the market. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
tool_result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.
